A self-directed curriculum · revised September 2026

The Engineer's Syllabus

Sixteen stages from your first line of code to the depth that makes you the person a team calls when the system is on fire. Every stage names what to learn, what to read, and what to ship.

Stages16
Directed study~2,720 h
At 20 h / week2.6 yr
Projects shipped15

How to use this

This is a map, not a schedule. The order is chosen so that each stage rests on something you already understand, which is why it is worth following even when a later stage looks more exciting. Seven rules decide whether you finish it.

If you already have a degree or a few years of work behind you, skip ahead to where to start and take the diagnostic first.

  • 01
    Build more than you read. Every stage below ends with something you ship. A stage is not finished when you have watched the lectures. It is finished when the project runs and someone other than you has used it.
  • 02
    Budget 100 to 200 hours per major subject. This is the figure the Teach Yourself Computer Science authors settled on, and it holds up. Anything under that produces recognition without understanding.
  • 03
    One language, all the way down, before a second. Depth in one language transfers. A shallow acquaintance with six does not. Pick Python or JavaScript and stay there until stage 07.
  • 04
    Never run more than two stages at once. Mathematics pairs well with algorithms. Craft pairs well with anything. Three concurrent subjects means three abandoned subjects.
  • 05
    Write about what you learn, in public. A learning log forces you to articulate the thing you half-understand. It is also, in practice, the strongest hiring signal a self-taught engineer can produce.
  • 06
    Let the assistant write code only after you can read it. Coding agents are leverage on a foundation and a liability without one. The rule that keeps you honest: you must be able to explain every line you ship.
  • 07
    Consistency beats intensity. Ten focused hours a week for three years outruns forty sporadic hours for six months. Protect the streak, not the session.

The prerequisite spine

Most of the curriculum is reorderable. These dependencies are not. Architecture is what makes operating systems and databases legible instead of memorised, and distributed systems are incoherent until you know what a process and a packet actually are.

Time budget

Hours below are study hours, not calendar time. They assume focused work with a project attached, not lectures playing in a browser tab.

Commitment First job (~1,070 h) Solid mid-level (~1,940 h) Senior depth (~2,720 h)
10 h / week2 years3 yr 9 mo5 yr 3 mo
20 h / week1 year1 yr 11 mo2 yr 7 mo
40 h / week6 months11 months1 yr 4 mo

One honest caveat. The last column buys you the knowledge of a senior engineer, not the title. Seniority also requires years of shipping alongside other people, absorbing production incidents, and being wrong in public. No reading list shortens that part.

Where to start if you have a degree

A computer science degree covers stages 01 through 08 and largely skips 09 through 15. You were taught what a B-tree is. You were probably never made to refactor someone else's code under test, deploy it, or be woken up when it failed. That gap is the whole of the applied half of this document, and it is what hiring screens for now.

So the short answer is stage 09, after a one-week sweep of stage 00. But a degree certifies attendance, not retention, and the course you took in second year has decayed. Verify rather than assume. Each test below is one question you can answer honestly in an afternoon, and failing one means that stage is not behind you.

StageCan you do this today, unaided?Typical graduate
00 ToolsRebase through a conflict, then explain what it did to the commit graphGap
01 ProgrammingBuild a tested command-line tool in an afternoon with no frameworkSolid
02 AlgorithmsSolve an unseen medium graph problem in thirty minutes with no referenceRusty
03 MathematicsProve an algorithm correct by inductionSolid
04 ArchitectureExplain why two loops of identical complexity differ fourfold in speedRusty
05 Operating systemsFind and fix a race condition in threaded code you did not writeRusty
06 NetworkingNarrate a request end to end, including the TLS handshakeRusty
07 CompilersWrite a recursive descent parser from memoryVaries
08 DatabasesRead an execution plan and name the index that is missingGap
09 Software craftRefactor a large unfamiliar codebase under test without changing behaviourGap
10 ShippingName something a stranger depends on that you built and still maintainGap
11 DistributedDesign for ten million users and defend your choice of shard keyGap
12 ProductionPoint to an incident you were paged for on something you deployedGap
13 SecurityDescribe a real broken access control bug you found yourselfGap
14 AI engineeringShow a model-backed feature you shipped with an automated eval suiteGap
Solid — skip the stage Rusty — refresher only, about a fifth of the hours Gap — the full stage at full hours

The compressed track

A stage you once passed takes roughly a fifth of the listed hours to restore. Re-read your notes, build the one project, and move on. Do not re-study from the top. That turns 2,720 hours into something closer to 1,640.

Sweep 00 – 08 400 h Refresher pace. Projects only, skip the lectures.
Full effort 09, 10, 12 680 h Craft, ship a product, then operate it in production.
Then 11, 13, 14 560 h Distributed systems, security, AI engineering.
Graduate total ~1,640 h 1 yr 7 mo at 20 h per week.

One warning specific to your position. Graduates tend to jump straight to stage 11, because distributed systems feels like the prestigious part and the coursework flattered it. It does not stick before you have operated something real. Kleppmann reads as trivia until you have been woken at three in the morning by a replication lag alert.

Stages 09, 10 and 12 are the whole distance between a computer science graduate and an employable engineer. Spend the 680 hours there first, in that order.

Milestone AYou can build things
stages 00 – 02, 09, 10

Roughly 1,070 hours. You can take a vague idea, decompose it, build it, test it, and put it in front of a user. This is the point where a junior role becomes realistic.

STAGE 00 Foundation

Tools, the shell, and how to learn

4 weeks60 hoursNo prerequisites

Almost nobody teaches this, and it quietly costs beginners hundreds of hours. Before you learn to program, learn to operate the machine you will program on. Every stage after this runs faster because of it.

What you learn

  • The shell as a language: pipes, redirection, globbing, exit codes, grep, find, sed, awk
  • The filesystem model: paths, permissions, symlinks, environment variables, PATH
  • Git as a data structure, not a list of commands: commits, trees, refs, branching, rebase, merge conflicts, bisect
  • Collaborating on GitHub: forks, pull requests, review comments, issues
  • One editor to fluency, with its keybindings, search, and multi-file navigation
  • Reading documentation and error messages instead of pasting them somewhere
  • Asking a question well: minimal reproduction, what you tried, what you expected
  • Study technique: spaced repetition for facts, deliberate practice for skills, retrieval over rereading

Resources

  • Course
    The Missing Semester of Your CS Education MIT · the single highest-leverage two weeks in this document
  • Book
    Pro Git Chacon & Straub · read chapters 1–3 and 7
  • Practice
    Learn Git Branching visual, interactive, fixes rebase anxiety
  • Book
    Make It Stick Brown, Roediger & McDaniel · how learning actually works

Ship this

A public dotfiles repository, plus one shell script that automates a chore you genuinely repeat. Write the README as if a stranger will use it.

STAGE 01 Foundation

Programming foundations

3–4 months300 hoursAfter stage 00

The longest single stage, and the one people rush hardest. The goal is not syntax. It is the ability to hold a problem in your head, break it into parts, and express those parts as code that someone else can read. Do not be the person who never quite understood recursion.

What you learn

  • Values, types, variables, expressions, statements, scope
  • Control flow, iteration, and the loop invariants that make it correct
  • Functions as the unit of abstraction: arguments, return values, purity, side effects
  • Recursion, base cases, the call stack, and why deep recursion blows up
  • Collections: lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples, and the cost of each operation
  • Strings, encodings, and why UTF-8 exists
  • Errors and exceptions: raising, catching, and failing loudly at the right boundary
  • Files, streams, serialisation, JSON and CSV
  • Objects and classes, composition, interfaces, and when not to use inheritance
  • Automated testing from week one, with a real test runner
  • Debugging with a debugger: breakpoints, stepping, inspecting state
  • Modules, packages, dependencies, virtual environments, lockfiles
  • Memory: the stack, the heap, references, mutation, and aliasing bugs
  • Reading unfamiliar code and changing it without breaking it

Resources

  • Course
    CS50x Harvard · start in C. The pointer chapter is the point
  • Course
    Berkeley CS 61A abstraction, recursion, interpreters · do this or SICP
  • Book
    Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs Abelson & Sussman · chapters 1–3 with exercises
  • Practice
    Exercism ~100 small problems with human mentorship
  • Course
    The Odin Project if the web is your destination, use this as the spine

Ship this

Four programs, each in a different shape. A command-line tool with arguments and a help screen. A program that reads messy real-world data and produces a clean report. A small game with state. A script that talks to a public API and caches its results.

Each with tests, a README, and no framework doing the thinking for you.

STAGE 02 Theory

Data structures and algorithms

3–4 months250 hoursAfter stage 01

This is the vocabulary of the field. Not because interviews ask for it, though they do, but because a problem you can name is a problem you can look up. Implement every structure once, from nothing, before you ever use the library version again.

What you learn

  • Asymptotic analysis: big-O, big-theta, amortised cost, space complexity
  • Arrays, dynamic arrays, and why appending is amortised constant time
  • Linked lists, stacks, queues, deques, circular buffers
  • Hash tables: hashing, collision resolution, load factor, resizing
  • Trees: binary search trees, balancing, heaps, priority queues, tries
  • Graphs: adjacency lists and matrices, BFS, DFS, topological sort, cycle detection
  • Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford, A*; minimum spanning trees
  • Union-find with path compression
  • Sorting: merge, quick, heap, insertion, counting and radix; stability; when each wins
  • Binary search and its off-by-one traps, including search over answer space
  • Recursion to divide-and-conquer to dynamic programming: memoisation, tabulation, state design
  • Greedy algorithms and the exchange argument that proves them
  • Backtracking, pruning, constraint problems
  • Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, monotonic stacks
  • Bit manipulation and its idioms
  • NP-completeness and reductions: recognising when no efficient answer exists
  • Probabilistic structures: Bloom filters, count-min sketch, HyperLogLog

Resources

  • Book
    The Algorithm Design Manual Skiena · the war stories are the reason to pick this over CLRS
  • Course
    MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms full lectures, notes and problem sets
  • Course
    Stanford Algorithms Tim Roughgarden · four-part specialisation
  • Practice
    NeetCode 150 a curated set beats grinding 500 random problems
  • Book
    Introduction to Algorithms CLRS · a reference to look things up in, not to read cover to cover

Ship this

A library implementing every structure above from scratch, with tests and complexity documented per method. Then solve around 150 curated problems, and for each one you fail, write down which pattern you missed.

STAGE 03 Theory

Mathematics for computing

2–3 months150 hoursRun in parallel with stage 02

Computer science is applied mathematics that got out of hand. You do not need a mathematics degree, but the discrete half is not optional, and proof by induction is the same muscle as recursion. Run this alongside algorithms, not before them.

What you learn

  • Logic and proof: implication, quantifiers, contradiction, and induction
  • Sets, relations, functions, equivalence classes, partial orders
  • Combinatorics: permutations, combinations, pigeonhole, inclusion–exclusion
  • Discrete probability: conditional probability, Bayes, expectation, variance, linearity of expectation
  • Common distributions and tail bounds; randomised algorithm analysis
  • Graph theory as mathematics: connectivity, colouring, matchings, planarity
  • Number theory: modular arithmetic, GCD, primes, and the road to public-key cryptography
  • Recurrence relations and the master theorem
  • Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, transformations, rank, eigenvectors
  • Calculus to the level of derivatives, gradients, and optimisation
  • Statistics you will actually use: sampling, confidence intervals, A/B tests, Simpson's paradox

Resources

  • Course
    MIT 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science Tom Leighton · lectures plus the free 1,000-page text
  • Video
    Essence of Linear Algebra 3Blue1Brown · watch before any linear algebra course
  • Course
    MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra Gilbert Strang
  • Book
    Think Stats Downey · statistics through code rather than notation

Ship this

Written solutions to two full 6.042J problem sets, including the proofs. Then a short simulation that demonstrates a counter-intuitive probability result, with the maths written up next to the code.

STAGE 04 Systems

Computer architecture

2–3 months150 hoursGateway to stages 05, 06, 08

Without a solid mental model of how the machine works, every higher abstraction you learn stays brittle. This is the stage that turns performance from superstition into arithmetic, and it unlocks operating systems and databases behind it.

What you learn

  • Number representation: binary, hex, two's complement, overflow
  • IEEE 754 floating point, and why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
  • Boolean logic, gates, multiplexers, adders, the ALU
  • Sequential logic: flip-flops, registers, the clock
  • Instruction set architecture, machine code, and reading assembly
  • The fetch-decode-execute cycle; a datapath and a control unit
  • The memory hierarchy: registers, L1/L2/L3, RAM, disk, and their real latencies
  • Cache lines, locality, associativity, and cache-friendly data layout
  • Pipelining, hazards, branch prediction, speculative execution
  • Instruction-level and data-level parallelism, SIMD
  • How a program becomes a process: compiling, assembling, linking, loading
  • The stack frame, calling conventions, and how buffer overflows happen
  • I/O, interrupts, DMA, the system bus

Resources

  • Course
    Nand2Tetris, parts I and II build a working computer from a NAND gate upward
  • Book
    Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective Bryant & O'Hallaron · if you read one systems book, this
  • Course
    Berkeley CS 61C Great Ideas in Computer Architecture
  • Book
    Computer Organization and Design Patterson & Hennessy · the RISC-V edition

Ship this

The full Nand2Tetris stack: gates, ALU, CPU, assembler, virtual machine, and a compiler for its language. It is the first project most people build that is complex enough to make software engineering feel necessary.

Then take one slow program and make it four times faster using only cache locality.

STAGE 05 Systems

Operating systems and concurrency

2–3 months150 hoursRequires stage 04

Every line of code you write is run by an operating system, and most production incidents are arguments with it. Concurrency lives here too, and it is the subject where confident guessing does the most damage.

What you learn

  • Processes: address space, fork and exec, process states, signals
  • Threads, context switching, kernel versus user mode, system calls
  • Scheduling: round robin, priority, multi-level feedback, fairness
  • Concurrency primitives: mutexes, semaphores, condition variables, atomics
  • Race conditions, deadlock, livelock, starvation, and the four Coffman conditions
  • Concurrency models beyond threads: event loops, async/await, actors, CSP channels
  • Virtual memory: paging, page tables, the TLB, page faults, swapping
  • Memory allocation, fragmentation, garbage collection strategies
  • File systems: inodes, directories, journalling, durability and fsync
  • I/O models: blocking, non-blocking, multiplexed, asynchronous; epoll and kqueue
  • Interprocess communication: pipes, sockets, shared memory, message queues
  • Virtualisation and containers: namespaces, cgroups, what Docker actually is

Resources

  • Book
    Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces Arpaci-Dusseau · free, excellent, the default choice
  • Course
    Berkeley CS 162 lectures that pair with OSTEP
  • Practice
    MIT 6.1810 and the xv6 labs a real teaching kernel you modify
  • Book
    The Little Book of Semaphores Downey · synchronisation puzzles that build intuition

Ship this

A shell that supports pipes, redirection, and job control. A thread pool with a work queue. Then complete the xv6 labs, adding at least one system call of your own.

STAGE 06 Systems

Networking and the web

6–8 weeks120 hoursRequires stage 04

Almost everything you build will be reached over a network, and almost every mysterious latency problem lives in this stage. Learn it top-down, starting from HTTP, which is where your work touches it.

What you learn

  • The layered model and encapsulation; what each layer is actually responsible for
  • HTTP in depth: methods, status codes, headers, caching, cookies, content negotiation
  • HTTP/2 multiplexing and HTTP/3 over QUIC; head-of-line blocking
  • TCP: the handshake, sequence numbers, retransmission, flow control, congestion control
  • UDP and when losing packets is the right trade
  • IP addressing, subnets, routing, NAT, IPv6
  • DNS: resolution, record types, TTLs, and why it is always DNS
  • TLS: handshake, certificates, chains of trust, certificate authorities, mTLS
  • Sockets: the API underneath every client and server you have used
  • Real-time transports: WebSockets, server-sent events, long polling, WebRTC
  • RPC over the network: gRPC, protocol buffers, schema evolution
  • CDNs, edge caching, anycast, and load balancers at layers 4 and 7
  • Network diagnosis: dig, traceroute, tcpdump, Wireshark, browser dev tools

Resources

  • Book
    Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach Kurose & Ross · do the Wireshark labs, they are the course
  • Course
    Stanford CS 144 the lab where you implement TCP is worth the whole stage
  • Book
    High Performance Browser Networking Ilya Grigorik · free online
  • Reference
    MDN HTTP reference the working reference you will return to for years

Ship this

An HTTP/1.1 server written directly on TCP sockets, handling keep-alive, chunked encoding and concurrent connections, with no web framework. Then implement a working TCP stack in the CS 144 labs.

STAGE 07 Systems

Languages, interpreters and compilers

6–8 weeks120 hoursRequires stages 01, 04

Understanding how a language is implemented makes every language easier to pick up and makes your own code better, because you stop guessing what the runtime does. It is also the most enjoyable stage in this document.

What you learn

  • Lexing, parsing, grammars, abstract syntax trees
  • Recursive descent and precedence climbing; parser generators and their trade-offs
  • Semantic analysis, scope resolution, symbol tables
  • Type systems: static and dynamic, strong and weak, inference, generics, variance
  • Tree-walking interpreters versus bytecode virtual machines
  • Intermediate representations, optimisation passes, code generation, register allocation
  • Runtime memory management: reference counting, tracing collectors, generational GC
  • Closures, first-class functions, tail calls, continuations
  • Paradigms compared: imperative, object-oriented, functional, logic
  • Immutability, algebraic data types, pattern matching, and what they buy you
  • Foreign function interfaces and language interoperation

Resources

  • Book
    Crafting Interpreters Bob Nystrom · free, beautifully written, do both halves
  • Course
    Stanford Compilers Alex Aiken
  • Book
    Compilers: Principles, Techniques and Tools the Dragon Book · cherry-pick chapters, do not read it straight through
  • Practice
    A second paradigm learn Haskell, OCaml, Elixir or Clojure until it changes how you write your first language

Ship this

A complete language: scanner, parser, resolver, tree-walking interpreter, then a bytecode virtual machine with its own garbage collector. Add one feature the book does not cover, so you have to design it yourself.

STAGE 08 Systems

Databases and data modelling

2–3 months180 hoursRequires stage 04

Data sits at the centre of almost every program worth writing, and very few engineers understand how the database actually executes their query. This stage pays for itself the first time you read an execution plan instead of adding an index at random.

What you learn

  • The relational model, keys, referential integrity, normal forms, and when to denormalise
  • SQL properly: joins, subqueries, CTEs, window functions, grouping sets, set operations
  • Indexes: B-trees, LSM trees, composite and covering indexes, selectivity, index-only scans
  • Query planning and execution: reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE, join strategies, statistics
  • Transactions and ACID; isolation levels; the anomalies each one permits
  • Concurrency control: two-phase locking, MVCC, optimistic concurrency, deadlock handling
  • Durability: write-ahead logging, checkpoints, crash recovery, replication lag
  • Storage engines: row stores versus column stores, page layout, compression
  • Schema design and safe online migrations under live traffic
  • NoSQL families: document, key-value, wide-column, graph, time-series, and the fit for each
  • Caching: Redis, cache-aside and write-through, TTLs, stampedes, invalidation
  • Full-text search and inverted indexes
  • Analytical data: OLTP versus OLAP, warehouses, star schemas, ETL and ELT
  • The object-relational mismatch, and where ORMs help and where they mislead

Resources

  • Course
    CMU 15-445 Database Systems Andy Pavlo · lectures and projects, all public
  • Book
    Use The Index, Luke Markus Winand · indexing explained for developers
  • Course
    Stanford Databases Jennifer Widom · the modelling and SQL modules
  • Book
    Designing Data-Intensive Applications, chapters 2–4 Kleppmann · storage, encoding and data models

Ship this

A key-value store with a write-ahead log, crash recovery, and a B-tree or LSM index. Then take a slow query in a real dataset of a million rows and bring it under fifty milliseconds, documenting each plan change.

Milestone BYou understand the machine
stages 00 – 08

Roughly 1,360 hours. You can reason about a program from the transistor to the HTTP response, and debug it at any layer in between. Most working engineers never reach this point. It is what separates competence from seniority later.

STAGE 09 Craft

Software craft and engineering practice

3–4 months220 hoursStart early, never finish

This is where a programmer becomes an engineer. Everything before this stage is about making code work. This stage is about making code that a team can change safely two years from now, which is the actual job.

What you learn

  • Naming, function size, and comments that explain why rather than what
  • Managing complexity: deep modules, narrow interfaces, information hiding
  • SOLID principles, read critically rather than as scripture
  • Composition over inheritance, dependency inversion, the seams that make code testable
  • Design patterns, and the far more useful skill of recognising when you do not need one
  • Testing: unit, integration, end-to-end; the test pyramid and its critics
  • Test-driven development, property-based testing, snapshot tests, mutation testing
  • Test doubles: fakes, stubs, mocks, and why over-mocking makes tests useless
  • Refactoring in small safe steps with tests as the net
  • Working with legacy code: characterisation tests, seams, strangler fig migrations
  • Code review: what to look for, how to disagree, how to receive it
  • Branching strategies, trunk-based development, feature flags, semantic versioning
  • Systematic debugging: bisect, reduce, hypothesise, verify. Profiling before optimising
  • Technical writing: READMEs, design documents, architecture decision records, RFCs
  • Estimation, decomposition, scope negotiation, and working in iterations honestly
  • Error handling strategy: where to fail, where to retry, what to log, what to surface

Resources

  • Book
    A Philosophy of Software Design Ousterhout · short, dense, the best book on complexity
  • Book
    The Pragmatic Programmer Hunt & Thomas · the 20th anniversary edition
  • Book
    Refactoring Martin Fowler · second edition
  • Book
    Working Effectively with Legacy Code Michael Feathers · for the job you will actually have
  • Reading
    Google's code review guidelines short, practical, free

Ship this

Take your worst earlier project and refactor it under a full test suite without changing behaviour. Then make three real pull requests to open-source projects and absorb the review comments without arguing first.

STAGE 10 Applied

Building and shipping real products

3–4 months240 hoursRequires stages 06, 08, 09

Everything so far has been components. This stage is the whole machine, with users, payments, mistakes, and things that break at three in the morning. The hiring market has moved decisively from "I helped on a feature" to "I built this and shipped it."

What you learn

  • API design: resources, HTTP semantics, status codes, idempotency, pagination, filtering
  • Versioning and backward compatibility; deprecation without breaking clients
  • GraphQL and gRPC, and the honest trade-offs against REST
  • Authentication and authorisation: sessions, tokens, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, refresh flows
  • Permission models: role-based, attribute-based, multi-tenancy and data isolation
  • Frontend fundamentals: semantic HTML, the CSS box and layout models, the DOM, the event loop
  • Accessibility as a requirement: keyboard navigation, focus, contrast, screen readers, ARIA
  • One component framework well, plus state management and data fetching patterns
  • Rendering strategies: client-side, server-side, static, streaming, hydration cost
  • Build tooling, bundling, code splitting, and the performance budget
  • Background work: job queues, workers, schedulers, retries, dead letter queues
  • Files and media: uploads, object storage, signed URLs, image pipelines, CDNs
  • Integrations: webhooks, third-party APIs, payments, transactional email
  • Rate limiting, pagination at scale, idempotency keys, and defensive input validation
  • Feature flags, analytics, and shipping to a subset of users first
  • Product thinking: what the user is trying to do, and what you can refuse to build

Resources

  • Course
    Full Stack Open University of Helsinki · modern, free, project-driven
  • Course
    The Odin Project the closest free thing to how a working developer learns
  • Reference
    roadmap.sh a checklist of the ecosystem, not a curriculum · use it to find gaps
  • Reference
    WCAG 2.2 quick reference accessibility as a specification, not an opinion

Ship this

One real product with real users. Accounts, a database, background jobs, payments or another irreversible action, and a deployment you maintain for at least three months.

Three to five polished projects beat twenty abandoned ones. Delete the rest.

STAGE 11 Systems

Distributed systems and architecture

4–6 months280 hoursRequires stages 05, 06, 08

Once a second machine is involved, everything you assumed about time, order and failure stops being true. This is the deepest stage in the curriculum and the one that most defines a senior engineer. Do not start it before you have built something real, or none of it will stick.

What you learn

  • Why distribute at all: throughput, availability, latency, and the cost of each
  • The eight fallacies of distributed computing, and how each one bites
  • Replication: single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless; synchronous and asynchronous trade-offs
  • Partitioning and sharding, rebalancing, consistent hashing, hot keys
  • Consistency models: linearizability, sequential, causal, eventual; read-your-writes
  • CAP and PACELC stated correctly, rather than as a slogan
  • Consensus: leader election, Raft, Paxos, quorums, split brain
  • Time and ordering: clock skew, logical clocks, vector clocks, hybrid clocks
  • Distributed transactions: two-phase commit, sagas, outbox pattern, idempotent consumers
  • Messaging: queues versus logs, Kafka, delivery semantics, and the exactly-once myth
  • Event-driven architecture, CQRS, event sourcing, and their real costs
  • Failure handling: timeouts, retries with jittered backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, backpressure
  • Load balancing, service discovery, health checks, graceful degradation
  • Batch and stream processing; windowing, watermarks, late data
  • Architecture styles: monolith, modular monolith, services, serverless, event-driven
  • Domain-driven design: bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language
  • The system design method: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high level, deep dive, bottlenecks

Resources

Ship this

Implement Raft, including leader election, log replication and persistence, and make it survive a partition test. Build a distributed rate limiter. Then write full design documents for five well-known systems and have someone senior tear them apart.

STAGE 12 Applied

Production, infrastructure and reliability

3–4 months220 hoursRequires stages 05, 06, 10

Code that is not running is not doing anything. This stage covers the distance between your laptop and a system that stays up, and it is where engineers who can operate what they build become disproportionately valuable.

What you learn

  • Linux in production: processes, systemd, users and permissions, resource limits, log locations
  • Diagnosing a sick box: top, iostat, ss, strace, perf, flame graphs
  • Containers: images, layers, Dockerfiles, multi-stage builds, Compose, registries
  • Orchestration: pods, deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets, autoscaling
  • Continuous integration and delivery: pipelines, caching, artefacts, gated merges
  • Deployment strategies: rolling, blue-green, canary, and safe rollback
  • Infrastructure as code: Terraform, state, modules, drift, plan review as code review
  • One cloud provider in depth: compute, object storage, networking and VPCs, IAM, managed databases
  • Observability: metrics with Prometheus, structured logs, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
  • Dashboards that answer a question, and alerts that a human should actually wake up for
  • Service level indicators, objectives and error budgets
  • Incident response: severity, comms, mitigation before diagnosis, blameless postmortems
  • Capacity planning, load testing, and reading a latency histogram rather than an average
  • Cost as an engineering constraint; the bill is a design document
  • Backups, restores you have actually tested, and disaster recovery objectives

Resources

    Site Reliability Engineering Google · all three volumes free online

Ship this

Take the product from stage 10 and put it on real infrastructure defined entirely in code, with a deployment pipeline, metrics, traces, two meaningful alerts, and a runbook. Then break it deliberately and write the postmortem.

STAGE 13 Craft

Security engineering

6–8 weeks120 hoursWoven through every stage above

Security is not a stage you complete, it is a lens you acquire. Concentrate it here once so that it becomes reflex, then apply it to everything you have already built. The exercises below are on deliberately vulnerable targets, which is the only place to practise.

What you learn

  • Threat modelling: assets, trust boundaries, attacker goals, STRIDE
  • The OWASP Top Ten in practice: broken access control, injection, XSS, SSRF, misconfiguration
  • Input validation and output encoding as distinct defences with distinct placement
  • Authentication done properly: Argon2 or bcrypt, salting, MFA, secure session lifecycle
  • Authorisation bugs, which are the most common serious flaw in real applications
  • Applied cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric, hashing, signing, key exchange, TLS
  • Why you use a vetted library and never design your own scheme
  • Secrets management, key rotation, and keeping credentials out of source control
  • Supply chain: dependency pinning, lockfiles, vulnerability scanning, provenance
  • Browser security model: same-origin policy, CORS, CSP, cookie attributes, CSRF tokens
  • Privacy engineering: data minimisation, retention, PII handling, GDPR obligations
  • Secure defaults, least privilege, and defence in depth as design principles

Resources

Ship this

Complete the PortSwigger labs for access control, injection and XSS. Then write a threat model for your own product, fix everything it surfaces, and add a dependency scan to the pipeline.

STAGE 14 Applied

AI engineering

2–3 months160 hoursRequires stages 03, 09, 10

Language models are now a component you integrate, like a database or a payment provider, and integrating them well is an engineering discipline with its own failure modes. The scarce skill is not prompting. It is evaluation: knowing whether the thing you shipped is actually working.

What you learn

  • How a language model works to a useful depth: tokens, context windows, attention, sampling
  • Embeddings and vector similarity; what they represent and where they mislead
  • Prompt engineering as interface design: structure, examples, decomposition, constrained output
  • Structured outputs and schema-validated responses your code can rely on
  • Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, indexing, hybrid search, reranking, citation
  • Tool use and function calling; agent loops, and recognising when an agent is the wrong shape
  • Evaluation: golden datasets, task-specific metrics, model-as-judge, regression suites in CI
  • Guardrails: prompt injection, jailbreaks, PII redaction, output filtering, human review gates
  • Cost and latency engineering: model routing, caching, batching, streaming, budgets per request
  • Observability for non-deterministic systems: tracing, sampling, replay, drift detection
  • Fine-tuning and distillation, and the narrow cases where they beat better prompting
  • Working with coding agents: writing the spec, reviewing the diff, keeping ownership of the code
  • Classical machine learning literacy: train and test splits, overfitting, metrics, baselines
  • The ethics that are also engineering: bias, attribution, disclosure, informed consent

Ship this

One AI feature inside the product from stage 10, with a golden dataset of at least fifty cases, an automated eval that runs in CI, tracing, a cost ceiling per request, and a documented fallback for when the model fails.

The eval suite is the deliverable. The feature is the excuse to build it.

Milestone CYou can be trusted with a system
stages 00 – 14

Roughly 2,720 hours. You can design a system, build it, secure it, deploy it, operate it, and explain every decision in it. From here the curriculum stops being a sequence and becomes a direction.

STAGE 15 Mastery

Expert practice

ContinuousThe rest of itRequires everything above

Expertise is not one more subject. It is depth in a chosen area, taste built from having been wrong, and the ability to move other engineers. The technical half of this is the easy half.

What you practise

  • Pick one track below and go three levels deeper than your team needs
  • Read primary sources: Dynamo, Bigtable, MapReduce, Spanner, Raft, The Google File System
  • Read production source code of tools you use daily, and fix something in one
  • Contribute to open source until you are trusted with review, not just patches
  • Write design documents that survive contact with sceptical senior engineers
  • Lead a project end to end: scoping, sequencing, risk, stakeholders, landing it
  • Mentor deliberately. Teaching is the fastest way to find the holes in your own model
  • Learn the business: what your company sells, what it costs, where engineering moves the number
  • Develop taste in trade-offs, which means being able to argue both sides honestly
  • Write publicly. A body of written work compounds more than any certification
  • Cultivate the boring virtues: reliability, clear communication, finishing things

A body of work rather than a project: a maintained open-source contribution, a written archive others cite, and at least one system in production that other engineers depend on and you did not build alone.

Where to specialise

Pick one after milestone B, not before. Breadth first makes the depth mean something, and every track below assumes the whole foundation underneath it.

Backend and distributed systems

Build the thing that stays up

The default track, and the one with the most demand. Depth in stages 08 and 11.

  • Storage engine internals
  • Consensus and replication in practice
  • Stream processing at scale
  • A systems language: Go or Rust

Platform and infrastructure

Build what other engineers build on

For people who like leverage more than features. Depth in stages 05 and 12.

  • Kubernetes internals and operators
  • Developer experience and build systems
  • Networking, service meshes, eBPF
  • Reliability engineering and capacity

AI engineering

Make non-deterministic systems dependable

The fastest-growing track. Depth in stages 03 and 14.

  • Retrieval and ranking quality
  • Evaluation and measurement design
  • Agent architectures and tool design
  • Inference cost and latency engineering

Low-level systems

Build the layers everyone assumes

Smallest job market, highest barrier, deepest satisfaction. Depth in stages 04, 05 and 07.

  • Kernels and drivers
  • Database and storage engines
  • Compilers and runtimes
  • Embedded and real-time systems

Product and frontend

Own what the user actually touches

Underrated, and the track closest to the business. Depth in stages 09 and 10.

  • Rendering and interaction performance
  • Accessibility and design systems
  • Offline, sync and local-first data
  • Experimentation and measurement

Security engineering

Find it before someone else does

Two distinct careers, offensive and defensive. Depth in stage 13.

  • Application and cloud security
  • Detection and incident response
  • Cryptographic engineering
  • Supply chain and software provenance

The ways this goes wrong

These are the failure modes that end self-directed study. Each one feels like progress while it is happening.

  • Tutorial hellFollowing along with a video produces the feeling of competence and none of it. The test is whether you can build a variation of the thing without the video. If not, you have not learned it.
  • Collecting languages and frameworksSix languages at a shallow depth is worth less than one at depth, and hiring managers stopped being impressed by long tool lists some years ago.
  • Skipping the foundations because the assistant writes the codeAn engineer who cannot evaluate generated code is a liability, and the market prices that correctly. Fundamentals are what make the leverage safe.
  • Reading the advanced book too earlyDesigning Data-Intensive Applications is transformative after you have built and operated something, and forgettable before. The same is true of most of the systems canon.
  • Optimising only for interviewsGrinding problems without building systems produces candidates who pass the screen and fail the job, which the industry has now adjusted for.
  • Never shipping to a real userA portfolio of unfinished projects signals the one thing employers screen hardest for. Finish three things completely rather than starting twenty.
  • Learning alone the whole wayCode review, pair programming and public work correct errors you cannot see from the inside. Find people, even if that means open source rather than a job.
  • Treating this document as a queueIt is a map. Loop back, re-read, and let a real problem pull you into a stage early when it does.

Companion volume · Stage 09 of The Engineer's Syllabus

The Engineer's Craft

Everything before this taught you to make code work. This volume is about making code that a team can still change safely two years from now: how to name it, shape it, test it, change it, review it, debug it, and write about it.

Chapters19
Code examples83
Exercises53
Stage budget220 h

How to use this volume

Every chapter has the same shape. It opens with its idea in one sentence, explains it through worked examples, lists the traps people fall into, and closes with exercises and a checklist you can apply to real code the same week.

The exercises matter more than the reading. Do them in your own editor, not in your head. Each has a solution folded underneath it: try first, then open it. Where your answer differs, decide whether it is worse or merely different. In this subject it is often the second.

Examples are in Python because it reads almost like pseudocode, but every idea transfers to other languages, and the text says so where a language feature changes the advice. Some early examples use floating-point numbers for money to stay short. Chapter 11 explains why real code must not.

Tick a chapter as read in its heading and the contents will track your progress. The marks are kept in this browser only.

The one question

Nearly everything in this volume answers one question: how expensive will the next change be?

Good names make the next change cheaper to understand. Deep modules let you change one thing without touching five. Tests make change safe, and refactoring stops its cost creeping upwards. Review, writing and estimation spread understanding across a team so no change depends on one person's memory.

When two pieces of advice conflict, and several in this book do, ask which one makes the next change cheaper for the next reader. That reader is usually you, six months from now, with none of today's context. The Pragmatic Programmer compresses the whole idea into three letters: ETC, easier to change.

Part I

Code that reads well

Code is read far more often than it is written. These four chapters are about the reader: the names they see first, the functions they step through, the comments that tell them what code cannot, and the shape of modules that let them understand one part without holding the whole system in their head.

Chapter 01

Naming

6 min read2 exercises

A name is the smallest unit of design. A good one is a compressed explanation. A bad one is a small lie that every future reader has to see through.

Why names carry so much weight

When you open an unfamiliar file, names are what you read first and most. You skim identifiers to build a map before you read a single expression. A precise name lets the reader skip the body entirely. A vague one forces them into it. A misleading one sends them the wrong way with confidence.

Naming is hard because it forces you to decide what a thing is. If you can't name a function without the word "and", or you can only reach for "manager" or "helper", the difficulty is usually telling you something about the design rather than about your vocabulary. Treat naming trouble as a design signal.

Principles that hold up

  • Name for intent, not for type or mechanism. pending_orders tells the reader what they are holding. order_list tells them only the container, and data tells them nothing at all.
  • Make length proportional to scope. A loop index that lives for two lines can be i. A constant read from forty files deserves a full, unambiguous name. Short names in wide scopes and long names in tiny ones are both mistakes.
  • Use the words your domain uses. If the finance team says an invoice is voided, write invoice.void(), not invoice.set_status(3). Domain-driven design calls this a ubiquitous language: the same terms in conversation, in tickets, and in code.
  • Put units in the name when the type doesn't carry them. timeout_seconds, price_cents, distance_km. In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team's software reported thrust in pound-force seconds and another's read it as newton-seconds.
  • Name booleans as predicates. is_active, has_shipped and can_retry read naturally after if. Avoid negatives: if not is_disabled makes every reader perform a double negation in their head.
  • Name functions for what they return or what they do. Queries are nouns or questions: total_price(), is_eligible(). Commands are verbs: send_invoice(), cancel_order(). A get_user() that also creates a user when one is missing is lying. Call it get_or_create_user().
  • One word per concept, one concept per word. If fetch, get, load and retrieve all mean "read from the database" in one codebase, readers will assume they differ. Pick one. Equally, don't let account mean a login in one module and a billing entity in another.
  • Avoid words that say nothing. data, info, item, manager, handler, processor, helper, util. Each is a placeholder for a decision not yet made. A UserManager usually turns out to be three things: a repository, a password policy, and a notification sender.

A worked example

Here is a function that works correctly and communicates nothing.

Nothing about the logic changed, and the function can now be understood without its call sites. Notice what the rename exposes, too. A boolean argument that switches what a function does is usually two functions sharing a body; chapter 2 comes back to that. Renaming often reveals design problems that bad names were hiding.

Renaming is cheap, so do it often

Modern editors rename safely across an entire codebase in seconds. Treat every name as a draft that improves as your understanding does. The moment you realise what a thing actually is, rename it, because otherwise that understanding is lost when you close the file.

The exception is names that escape your codebase: public API fields, database columns, event names, configuration keys. Those are contracts with other people, and chapter 14 covers how to change them.

Common traps
  • Names that encode the whole implementation. is_least_relevant_multiple_of_larger_prime_factor came up in a public exchange between John Ousterhout and Robert Martin. It is precise and nearly unreadable. When a name gets that long, the idea probably wants a comment or a better abstraction.
  • Private abbreviations. cstmr_acct_bal saves eight keystrokes and costs every reader a decoding step. Widely known abbreviations such as id, url and http are fine.
  • Names that drift. A send_email that now also writes an audit record has a stale name. Stale names are worse than vague ones, because readers trust them.
  • Cute names. yeet_order() is funny once, to one person.
Exercises
Exercise 1.1Critique the names

Each name below has a problem. Say what it is and propose a better name. Assume a small online shop.

data = fetch_orders(status="pending")                          # 1
flag = response.status_code in (502, 503, 504)                 # 2
def process_user(user): ...   # deactivates the account and emails the owner   # 3
TIMEOUT = 30                                                   # 4
if not is_not_verified: ...                                    # 5
def get_customer(email): ...  # inserts a new row when none is found           # 6
class OrderManager: ...       # loads orders, prices them, sends receipts      # 7
newsletter_recipient_email_addresses_list = []                 # 8
Show solution
  1. data says nothing. Use pending_orders.
  2. The flag means "this failure is worth retrying". Use is_retryable.
  3. process hides two actions. Name the behaviour, deactivate_and_notify(user), and consider splitting it, because the "and" is a design smell.
  4. The unit is missing. Use TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30.
  5. A double negative. Rename the variable is_verified and write if is_verified:.
  6. The name hides a side effect. Use get_or_create_customer(email).
  7. Three responsibilities in one name. Split into an OrderRepository, a price_order function, and a ReceiptSender.
  8. Too long, and the plural already implies a list. Use newsletter_recipients.
Exercise 1.2Rename without changing logic

Rename everything in this function so it can be understood without its call sites. Don't change the logic. Hint: a is a login attempt.

def chk(u, lst, n):
    c = 0
    for a in lst:
        if a.uid == u.id and a.ok is False:
            c += 1
    return c >= n
Show solution
def has_too_many_failed_logins(user, login_attempts, max_failures):
    failures = 0
    for attempt in login_attempts:
        if attempt.user_id == user.id and attempt.succeeded is False:
            failures += 1
    return failures >= max_failures

With good names, a simplification becomes visible that was invisible before: the loop is a count, and could be a sum() over a generator.

One trap is worth noticing. The original tests a.ok is False, which excludes None. If an attempt can have an unknown outcome, rewriting it as not attempt.succeeded would count unknowns as failures and change behaviour. A rename must never change logic, so check before you tidy.

Checklist
  • Can a reader tell what each name holds or does without reading its definition?
  • Does every boolean read naturally after if?
  • Are units in the name wherever the type doesn't carry them?
  • Is there exactly one word for each concept in this module?
  • Did you rename the things you now understand better than when you named them?
Go deeper

    A Philosophy of Software Design John Ousterhout · the chapter on choosing names
  • Book
    Domain-Driven Design Eric Evans · the origin of "ubiquitous language"
  • Free

Chapter 02

Functions

7 min read3 exercises

A function should do one thing, at one level of abstraction, and its signature should tell a caller everything they need without opening the body.

What "one thing" means

The rule is old and usually misread as "short". A better test is whether you can describe what the function does in one sentence without the word "and". If you can, it probably does one thing, whatever its length. If the sentence needs "validates the cart and charges the card and emails a receipt", you have three functions sharing a body.

The second test is levels of abstraction. A function that reads like a sequence of business steps shouldn't suddenly drop into string slicing or HTTP details. Mixing levels forces the reader to change zoom constantly.

checkout now reads as the four steps of the process, and each step can be understood, tested and changed alone. price takes now as an argument instead of reading the clock itself, which makes it deterministic; chapter 6 explains why that matters so much. The payment and email details moved behind payments.charge and send_receipt, where they live with the rest of their kind.

How long is too long?

There is no line count. Robert Martin argues for functions of a handful of lines. John Ousterhout argues that aggressive splitting produces conjoined functions that can only be understood together, so a reader must jump between five of them to follow a single idea. They debated this in public and did not converge.

The useful synthesis is two questions. Can a caller use this function without reading its body? Can a reader understand this function without reading the functions it calls? When splitting a function makes either answer worse, don't split it.

Arguments

  • Fewer is better. Every parameter is something a caller must understand and supply. Zero to three is comfortable. More usually means some of them belong together.
  • Flag arguments are two functions in disguise. render(invoice, True) means nothing at the call site. Split it into render_draft and render_final, or at least make the flag keyword-only so the call reads render(invoice, draft=True).
  • Group parameters that travel together. If street, city, postcode, country appear in five signatures, they are an Address. Introducing that object is one of the most common refactorings in chapter 11.
  • Don't mutate your arguments unless the name says so. A caller who passes a list to total_of(items) does not expect to find it sorted afterwards.

Commands and queries

Bertrand Meyer's command-query separation says a function should either change state or return information, never both. A query can be called any number of times without consequence, so it is safe in a log line, a debugger or a test. A command's name warns you that something happens.

Functions that do both surprise people: a get_next_invoice_number() that also increments a counter, or an is_valid() that records the check. The standard library breaks the rule where it's genuinely convenient, list.pop() being the famous case, and that's fine as long as the name makes the side effect obvious.

Guard clauses over nesting

Each special case is handled and dismissed at the top, and the main path runs unindented to the end. The reader never has to track which else belongs to which if.

Functional core, imperative shell

Gary Bernhardt's name for a structure that makes most code easy to test. Put decisions in pure functions that take values and return values: no clock, no network, no database. Wrap them in a thin outer layer that gathers inputs, calls the core, and performs the effects. The core is where the bugs would be, and it needs no mocks to test. The shell is so simple it barely needs testing at all.

Common traps
  • Extracting until nothing is left. Ten three-line functions that each call the next are harder to follow than one thirty-line function. Inline them back.
  • Names that restate the body. Extracting x > 0 and y > 0 into check_x_and_y() adds a jump and no meaning. is_in_first_quadrant() adds meaning.
  • Hidden state threading. Helpers that read and write instance variables set by other helpers are conjoined. Pass values explicitly.
  • Returning None for failure. Every caller must remember to check, and the ones who forget crash later, far from the cause. Raise instead. Chapter 16 covers this.
Exercises
Exercise 2.1Flatten with guard clauses

Rewrite this so the main path is unindented. Behaviour must not change.

def can_publish(post, user):
    if user is not None:
        if user.is_active:
            if post.author_id == user.id or user.is_editor:
                if not post.is_locked:
                    return True
                else:
                    return False
            else:
                return False
        else:
            return False
    else:
        return False
Show solution
def can_publish(post, user):
    if user is None or not user.is_active:
        return False
    if post.is_locked:
        return False
    return post.author_id == user.id or user.is_editor

Checking is_locked before ownership changes nothing here, because both paths return False. In general, though, reordering guards can change which error a caller sees, so verify equivalence rather than assuming it. A quick way is a table-driven test over every combination of inputs, run against both versions.

Exercise 2.2Spot the separation violations

Which of these break command-query separation, and what would you rename or split?

def next_order_number(self):
    self._counter += 1
    return f"ORD-{self._counter:06d}"

def is_valid(self, coupon):
    coupon.times_checked += 1
    return coupon.expires_at > self.clock.now()

def total(self):
    return sum(line.amount for line in self.lines)
Show solution
  • next_order_number changes state and returns a value, but "next" signals consumption, much like pop. It's an acceptable exception. Renaming it allocate_order_number() makes the command even clearer.
  • is_valid is the real problem: a query's name hiding a side effect. Calling it in a log line or a debugger changes data. Remove the counter update from it, or move that into an explicit record_check(coupon) command.
  • total is a pure query. It's fine.
Exercise 2.3Separate the core from the shell

Extract a pure function that decides who to notify and with what message, then write a test for it that needs no database and no mailer.

def notify_expiring_subscriptions():
    today = date.today()
    for sub in db.query("SELECT * FROM subscriptions WHERE active"):
        days_left = (sub.ends_on - today).days
        if days_left in (7, 1):
            mailer.send(sub.email, f"Your plan ends in {days_left} day(s).")
Show solution
def expiry_notices(subscriptions, today):
    notices = []
    for sub in subscriptions:
        days_left = (sub.ends_on - today).days
        if days_left in (7, 1):
            notices.append((sub.email, f"Your plan ends in {days_left} day(s)."))
    return notices


def notify_expiring_subscriptions(db, mailer, today):
    for email, message in expiry_notices(db.active_subscriptions(), today):
        mailer.send(email, message)


def test_notices_go_out_seven_days_and_one_day_before_expiry():
    today = date(2026, 3, 1)
    subs = [
        Sub("a@x.com", ends_on=date(2026, 3, 8)),   # 7 days away
        Sub("b@x.com", ends_on=date(2026, 3, 2)),   # 1 day away
        Sub("c@x.com", ends_on=date(2026, 3, 5)),   # 4 days away: no notice
    ]
    assert expiry_notices(subs, today) == [
        ("a@x.com", "Your plan ends in 7 day(s)."),
        ("b@x.com", "Your plan ends in 1 day(s)."),
    ]

The test needs no mocks, no database and no patched clock. That is the entire payoff of the pattern.

Checklist
  • Can you describe each function in one sentence without "and"?
  • Does each function stay at one level of abstraction?
  • Are there boolean flags at call sites that should be keyword-only, or separate functions?
  • Do any queries have side effects?
  • Is the decision-making code pure, with I/O pushed to the edges?

Chapter 03

Comments

6 min read2 exercises

Comments should say what the code cannot: why a decision was made, what an interface promises, and what a reader would otherwise have to learn the hard way.

The disagreement worth understanding

Few topics split experienced engineers like comments. Robert Martin treats a comment as a small failure: a sign the code didn't express itself, and a liability that will drift out of date. John Ousterhout treats comments as essential. Code can say what happens, but it cannot say why, and it cannot describe an abstraction without the reader reading its implementation. Their public exchange ended with each holding the opposite default: Martin distrusts a comment until it proves useful, and Ousterhout assumes it helps until it proves wasteful.

Both are right, about different kinds of comment. Comments that narrate what the code does are noise, and Martin's instinct is correct for them. Comments that describe an interface or record a reason are irreplaceable, and Ousterhout's instinct is correct there. The skill is telling the kinds apart.

Comments worth writing

KindWhat it saysExample
InterfaceWhat a function promises its caller: inputs, output, errors, side effectsA docstring on a public function
WhyThe reason for a decision that looks wrong or arbitrary"Retry twice: the provider returns 502s for about a second during their deploys."
WarningA consequence the reader must know before changing the code"Not thread-safe. Callers must hold the order lock."
ReferenceWhere the full explanation livesA link to the spec, the ticket, or the paper
IntentThe idea behind code that can only execute it"Both lists are sorted, so advance whichever head is smaller."

And the comments worth deleting:

  • Narration. # loop over the orders above for order in orders:.
  • Commented-out code. Version control remembers it. Nobody will ever be sure it's safe to delete, so everybody leaves it, forever.
  • Journal comments. Change history belongs in commit messages, where it's attached to the change.
  • Banners. # ===== HELPERS ===== usually means the file wants to be two files.
  • Apologies. # sorry, hack without saying what the hack works around. Replace it with a why comment and a ticket link.

Write the interface comment first

Ousterhout suggests writing the interface comment before the implementation. It works as a design tool: if the comment is long, full of conditions and caveats, the abstraction is probably wrong, and it's cheaper to find out before the code exists. A good interface comment describes what, never how. The how belongs to the implementation, which must stay free to change.

Every narration comment is gone, and the body is no harder to read without them. The docstring now tells a caller three things the code alone could not: that failure leaves state unchanged, what the reservation's lifecycle is, and the locking rule. None of that is visible in seven lines of implementation.

The comment that protects a fence

G. K. Chesterton described a fence across a road. A reformer wants it removed because he can see no use for it. The wiser reply: go and find out why it was put there, and then you may take it down. Code is full of fences, such as an odd sleep, a check that looks redundant, or a sort that seems unnecessary. A one-line why comment is the difference between the next engineer understanding the fence and removing it in a cleanup that brings back a production bug from three years ago.

Common traps
  • Docstrings that repeat the types. sku (str): the sku adds nothing a type hint doesn't. Describe meaning, units and constraints instead: "a catalogue SKU, case-sensitive".
  • Stale comments. A comment the code has outgrown is worse than none. Review comments as carefully as the code beside them.
  • Comments excusing bad names. x = 86400 # seconds in a day should be SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400.
  • Explaining how in an interface comment. It couples callers to the implementation you'll want to change later.
Exercises
Exercise 3.1Keep, delete or rewrite

For each comment, decide and give a reason.

# 1
i += 1  # increment i

# 2
# Use a set: this runs per request and the blocklist has ~50k entries.
blocked = set(load_blocklist())

# 3
# old approach
# for u in users: send(u)

# 4
time.sleep(0.2)  # wait

# 5
# Returns None if the user doesn't exist.
def find_user(email): ...

# 6
# TODO fix this
Show solution
  1. Delete. Pure narration.
  2. Keep. It records why a set was chosen, with the numbers that justify it. A reader who "simplifies" it to a list would make every request slower.
  3. Delete. Commented-out code. Version control has it.
  4. Rewrite. The code already says it waits. Say why, and why this long: "The label printer drops jobs sent within ~150 ms of each other."
  5. Keep, and move it into the docstring. It's interface information. Better still, declare the return type as User | None so the type checker enforces it.
  6. Rewrite. Say what's wrong and link a ticket: "TODO(INV-412): rounding is per line; finance wants rounding on the invoice total."
Exercise 3.2Write the interface comment

Write the docstring a caller needs. Describe behaviour, not implementation.

def merge_customer_records(primary_id, duplicate_id):
    primary = repo.get(primary_id)
    dup = repo.get(duplicate_id)
    for order in repo.orders_of(dup.id):
        order.customer_id = primary.id
        repo.save(order)
    primary.loyalty_points += dup.loyalty_points
    if not primary.phone:
        primary.phone = dup.phone
    repo.save(primary)
    repo.delete(dup.id)
Show solution
def merge_customer_records(primary_id: int, duplicate_id: int) -> None:
    """Fold a duplicate customer into the primary record, then delete it.

    Every order of the duplicate is reassigned to the primary and loyalty
    points are summed. The duplicate's phone number is kept only if the
    primary has none; all its other fields are discarded.

    Irreversible: the duplicate record is deleted. Both ids must exist.
    Not atomic: if it fails part way, some orders may already have moved,
    so call it inside a transaction.
    """

Writing this surfaces two design questions that the code hides: should this be atomic on its own, and is silently discarding the duplicate's other fields acceptable? That's the comment doing design work before anyone has been hurt by the answer.

Checklist
  • Does every public function have an interface comment that says what, not how?
  • Is there a why comment on every line that looks wrong but isn't?
  • Did you delete narration, commented-out code and journal comments?
  • Do the comments still match the code after your change?

Chapter 04

Complexity and deep modules

8 min read3 exercises

Complexity is anything that makes a system hard to understand or change. The strongest defence is the deep module: a lot of functionality behind a small, simple interface.

What complexity looks like

John Ousterhout defines complexity by its effects, which makes it recognisable in practice. It shows up in three ways.

  • Change amplification. A simple change requires edits in many places. Changing the currency symbol means touching forty templates.
  • Cognitive load. How much a developer must hold in mind to make a change safely. A function that only works if you remember to call init() first and flush() afterwards has high cognitive load.
  • Unknown unknowns. It isn't obvious which code must change, or what you need to know to change it. This is the worst of the three, because you can't see the cost until something breaks.

Its two root causes are dependencies, where code can't be understood or changed in isolation, and obscurity, where important information isn't obvious. Most of the rest of this volume is about reducing one or the other.

Deep and shallow modules

Picture every module as a rectangle. The top edge is its interface: everything a caller must learn to use it. The area beneath is the functionality it provides. A deep module has a narrow top and a large area. It gives a lot and asks little. A shallow module has a wide top and a small area, and its interface costs nearly as much to learn as its implementation would to write.

Unix file I/O is the classic deep module. Five calls, open, read, write, lseek and close, hide disk layout, caching, permissions, device drivers and concurrent access. A class whose methods each forward to one method on another class is the classic shallow module: an interface to learn, and nothing behind it.

A worked example: a rate limiter

Both implement the same token bucket. In the shallow design, every endpoint repeats five lines of algorithm, and a caller who forgets refill or save_bucket gets a limiter that is subtly wrong. Switch to a sliding window and you edit every caller: change amplification. The deep design hides the algorithm, the storage, the clock and the locking behind one method. The interface got smaller, and the module got more powerful.

Information hiding, and how it leaks

David Parnas made the case in 1972: divide a system by the design decisions most likely to change, and give each module one decision to hide. The opposite is information leakage, where one decision is reflected in several modules. If both the CSV exporter and the CSV importer know the column order, changing the format means changing both, and nothing forces you to remember.

A common cause is temporal decomposition: structuring code by the order things happen. A read step, a parse step and a write step feel natural, but if reading and writing both need to know the file format, the format leaks into both. Structure by knowledge, not by time. One module owns the format and offers both directions.

Pull complexity downwards

When complexity is unavoidable, it's better for the module to absorb it than to push it onto every caller. A module has one author and many users. Sensible defaults, handling common edge cases internally, and retrying transient failures are all ways of pulling complexity down. A configuration option for something the module could work out itself does the opposite: it pushes a decision onto every user.

Define errors out of existence

Every error a module can raise is part of its interface, and every caller must deal with it. Sometimes the cheapest fix is to redefine the operation so the error can't happen. Python's standard library has good examples.

Each one takes a case that would otherwise be an exception and gives it a sensible meaning. The same move works in your own code: make unsubscribe succeed when the user is already unsubscribed, and every caller loses a try block. Use judgement, though. Some errors must stay loud, like a payment that failed.

Tactical and strategic programming

Tactical programming aims to get the current feature working as fast as possible. Each shortcut is small and seems reasonable, and complexity accumulates one reasonable decision at a time. Strategic programming treats working code as necessary but not sufficient: the goal is a good design that also works. Ousterhout suggests investing something like ten to twenty percent of development time in design improvements. It pays back within months, because every later change is cheaper.

Common traps
  • Classitis. Splitting everything into tiny classes because small feels good produces many shallow modules, each with an interface to learn and little behind it.
  • Pass-through methods. A method that only calls another method with the same signature adds interface without adding depth. Merge the layers, or give each a distinct job.
  • Configuration as an escape hatch. Every option you expose is a decision every user must now make.
  • Pretending abstractions don't leak. Joel Spolsky's law says all non-trivial abstractions leak to some degree. Design for the leaks you can't avoid, such as network failure, and document them in the interface.
Exercises
Exercise 4.1Make it deep

This module makes every caller manage a connection. Redesign its interface so callers can't get it wrong. Write the new signatures and one example call.

class Mailer:
    def connect(self): ...
    def authenticate(self, user, password): ...
    def build_message(self, to, subject, body): ...
    def send_message(self, message): ...
    def disconnect(self): ...


# Every caller:
m = Mailer()
m.connect()
m.authenticate(SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD)
msg = m.build_message(customer.email, "Your receipt", body)
m.send_message(msg)
m.disconnect()
Show solution
class Mailer:
    """Sends email through the configured SMTP relay. Connections are
    opened, reused and closed internally. Transient failures are retried
    up to 3 times before MailDeliveryError is raised."""

    def __init__(self, host: str, user: str, password: str): ...

    def send(self, to: str, subject: str, body: str) -> None: ...


# Every caller:
mailer.send(customer.email, "Your receipt", body)

Credentials are supplied once, when the application is wired together. Connections, message building and retries are hidden. The caller's cognitive load drops from five ordered steps to one call, and the forgotten-disconnect() bug is gone because it can no longer be written.

Exercise 4.2Define the error away

This function raises in a case that callers nearly always treat as success. Redesign it.

def remove_from_cart(cart, sku):
    if sku not in cart.items:
        raise ItemNotInCart(sku)
    del cart.items[sku]
Show solution

Make removal idempotent. Removing an item that isn't there leaves the cart exactly as the caller wanted it:

def remove_from_cart(cart, sku):
    cart.items.pop(sku, None)

If some caller genuinely needs to know whether anything was removed, return a boolean rather than raising. Most callers will ignore it, which is exactly what they want.

Exercise 4.3Find the leak

Two modules share a design decision. Name it, and restructure so only one module knows it.

# signup.py
def create_user(email, password):
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    digest = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt, 600_000)
    db.insert_user(email, salt + digest)

# login.py
def check_password(user, password):
    salt, digest = user.password_hash[:16], user.password_hash[16:]
    candidate = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt, 600_000)
    return hmac.compare_digest(candidate, digest)
Show solution

The leaked decision is the password storage format: the algorithm, the iteration count, the salt length and the byte layout. Both modules know all four. Raise the iteration count in one and every login breaks.

# passwords.py: the only module that knows the storage format.
ITERATIONS = 600_000
SALT_BYTES = 16


def hash_password(password: str) -> bytes:
    salt = os.urandom(SALT_BYTES)
    return salt + _derive(password, salt)


def verify_password(password: str, stored: bytes) -> bool:
    salt, digest = stored[:SALT_BYTES], stored[SALT_BYTES:]
    return hmac.compare_digest(_derive(password, salt), digest)


def _derive(password: str, salt: bytes) -> bytes:
    return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt, ITERATIONS)

A production version should also record the algorithm and iteration count inside the stored hash, so the parameters can be upgraded without breaking existing passwords. Encoded formats such as Argon2's do exactly that, which is one more reason to use a vetted library here.

Checklist
  • For each module you touched, is its interface much simpler than its implementation?
  • Would changing one design decision touch one module, or several?
  • Did you push onto callers a decision the module could have made?
  • Can any error you raise be defined out of existence?
  • Did part of this change improve the design, or did it only add to it?
