Part V

In production

Four chapters on running an AI feature once it's live: the guardrails that contain a non-deterministic component, the cost and latency engineering that keeps it affordable and fast, the observability that lets you debug something that's different every time, and the narrow cases where fine-tuning earns its keep.

Chapter 14

Guardrails and safety

8 min read3 exercises

You can't prove a probabilistic model will never misbehave, so stop trying to make it perfectly behaved and make misbehaviour cheap to contain. Check what goes in, check what comes out, keep sensitive data out of both, and put a human in front of anything that matters. You own the output, whatever the model does.

You own the output

The starting point is legal and reputational, not technical. In 2024 a tribunal held Air Canada liable for wrong advice its chatbot gave a customer, rejecting the idea that the bot was a separate entity. In 2025 Deloitte refunded part of a contract after an AI-drafted report contained invented citations. The model's mistakes are your mistakes, so "the AI said it" is not a defence, and guardrails are how you keep the model's jagged behaviour from becoming your liability. The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 20, covered the security of AI features, prompt injection, the lethal trifecta, agents acting with too much authority; this chapter is the production-engineering side: the checks you run on every request and response.

Input guardrails

Before text reaches the model, run cheap checks. Bound the length and shape, as you would any input. Strip or redact data that shouldn't leave your systems, because a prompt sent to a model provider leaves your systems, and so does anything you log:

The redactor masks an email, a phone number and a real card number, but leaves a Luhn-invalid sixteen-digit reference alone, because masking everything that looks like a number is as bad as masking nothing. Run it before sending anything to a third-party model and before writing anything to a log (The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 19, on privacy). The injection check is deliberately modest: as the UK's NCSC put it, prompt injection may never be fully preventable, so a pattern match is a weak signal that raises review or routes to a limited-capability path, never a claim that the input is now safe. The real defence against injection is the capability limits of chapter 8 and Citadel chapter 20, not a regex.

Output guardrails

Because the model is non-deterministic, you can't guarantee by construction that it will never say a forbidden thing; you check what it actually said before the user sees it. The output guard above blocks a response that leaks an email address not in the allowed context, catching the model volunteering someone else's data, and one that makes a disallowed claim ("guaranteed returns", "this is financial advice"). Real systems layer more: a moderation classifier or a dedicated guard model (such as Llama Guard) for unsafe content, checks that the answer is grounded in its cited sources (chapter 7), and format and policy checks. None is perfect, which is why they're layered, defence in depth, the same principle as everywhere in security.

Jailbreaks, and why no prompt fixes them

Users will try to talk the model out of its instructions, "pretend you have no rules", role-play framings, encoded requests. Treating this as a prompt-writing contest ("add a firmer system prompt") loses, because there's always another phrasing. Handle it structurally: the model simply shouldn't have the capability to do the harmful thing, so even a successful jailbreak reaches nothing dangerous. A jailbroken customer-service bot that has no tool to issue refunds, read other accounts or send arbitrary email can be made to say rude things, embarrassing, but not to cause damage. Limit the blast radius and the jailbreak stops mattering.

The human gate, for what matters

For high-stakes output, the right guardrail is a person. Anything irreversible or consequential, money moving, an email leaving the company, medical or legal advice, a public statement, content about a named individual, should be reviewed before it takes effect, which is the Explicit-permission rule from the start of The Engineer's Citadel. The Deloitte report is what skipping that gate looks like. Design the human step to be fast and well-targeted: use the model to draft and the eval to triage, so humans spend their attention on the cases that need it, not on rubber-stamping everything. And always have a fallback for when the model fails, times out, trips a guardrail or returns low confidence, which is this stage's deliverable in miniature: a documented path that degrades to a safe default, a canned response, or a human.

Common traps
  • Believing a system prompt makes the model safe. Jailbreaks and injection route around it.
  • Sending or logging raw PII to a third-party model.
  • No output check, so the first time the model says something forbidden, a user sees it.
  • Treating a regex as injection "prevention" rather than a weak signal.
  • No human gate and no fallback for high-stakes or failed requests.
Exercises
Exercise 14.1Design the guardrails

A bank is adding an assistant that answers account questions and can initiate transfers. List the input guardrails, output guardrails and human gates you'd require.

Show solution
  • Input: authenticate and scope to the user's own accounts; redact nothing (it's their data) but never let the prompt reference another account; length limits; route suspected injection to a read-only path.
  • Output: block any response that mentions another customer's data; block financial-advice claims; check figures against the account record (don't trust the model's arithmetic, chapter 1); ground every factual claim in retrieved account data.
  • Human (or hard) gate: transfers require explicit user confirmation of amount and destination, and anything above a threshold or to a new payee requires step-up authentication; the model proposes, it never executes. Idempotency so a retry can't double-transfer.
  • Fallback: on any guardrail trip or low confidence, hand off to a human agent rather than guessing.
Exercise 14.2Why the regex isn't enough

A teammate proposes blocking prompt injection with a blocklist of phrases like "ignore previous instructions". Give two ways it's bypassed and the right framing.

Show solution

Bypasses are endless: rephrasing ("disregard what you were told above", "new rules for this task"), other languages, encoding (base64, leetspeak), or hiding the instruction in retrieved content or a tool result rather than the user's message (indirect injection, The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 20). The right framing is that injection detection is a weak, best-effort signal, useful for monitoring and for routing suspicious requests to a limited path, not a control you can rely on. The control that works is limiting what the model can do: narrow tools, no access to data the user shouldn't see, a human gate on actions. Then a successful injection reaches nothing worth protecting.

Exercise 14.3Place the human

For each feature, decide whether output can go straight to the user, needs an automated guardrail, or needs human review.

  1. Suggesting three related help articles.
  2. Drafting a legal letter sent on the company's behalf.
  3. Auto-replying to customer emails.
  4. Summarising a document for the user who uploaded it.
Show solution
  1. Straight through, with a light relevance check. A wrong suggestion is low-harm and the user chooses.
  2. Human review, always. It's legal, external and on the company's behalf, the Deloitte and Air Canada risk; the model drafts, a lawyer approves.
  3. Automated guardrails plus a gate for risky categories: safe for simple acknowledgements, but route refunds, complaints, legal or distressed messages to a human. An auto-reply is a public statement you own.
  4. Straight through, with a grounding check, since it's shown only to the person who provided the source and is low-stakes, though a "verify against the document" note is worth adding.
Checklist
  • Is PII redacted before it reaches a third-party model or a log?
  • Is every response checked before the user sees it, for leaks and disallowed content?
  • Is safety enforced by limiting capability, not just by the system prompt?
  • Does anything irreversible or high-stakes pass through a human?
  • Is there a documented fallback for when the model fails or a guardrail trips?

Chapter 15

Cost and latency engineering

8 min read3 exercises

An AI feature's bill and its speed are engineering outputs you control, not fixed properties of the model. The biggest wins come from sending fewer tokens, using the smallest model that passes your eval, caching the stable parts, and never letting a single request run away. Measure cost and latency as first-class metrics, because a feature that's too slow or too expensive doesn't ship.

Where the money goes

You pay per token, input and output priced separately, with output usually several times dearer per token because it's generated one at a time. But in most applications the input dominates the bill, because the context, system prompt, tools, retrieved documents, history, is large and the answer is small (the chapter 1 exercise showed a document request where input was three-quarters of the cost). So the first lever is almost always send fewer input tokens: retrieve less and sharper (Part III), cache the stable prefix (chapter 5), trim history. The levers, in rough order of impact:

Route to the smallest model that passes

Models differ in price by more than tenfold, and most requests don't need the most capable one. A cascade (or router) sends every request to a small, cheap model first and escalates to a big model only the ones that need it, detected by the small model's confidence, a difficulty classifier, or a cheap verification step. The example runs 10,000 requests through a small model and re-runs the 20% hardest on a big one: even paying twice for those, it costs 72% less than sending everything to the big model. The catch is quality, and it's exactly what your eval is for: the cascade is only sound if the small model is good enough on the slice it handles, which you measure, not assume. Get that wrong and you've saved money by shipping worse answers, which the eval would have caught.

Cache and batch

Two provider features cut cost with almost no downside. Prompt caching bills the unchanged prefix at a steep discount on repeat (chapter 5), 46% off even in the partial example above, far more in a chat loop where the whole system prompt and tools repeat. The batch API halves the price again for work that tolerates a day's latency, bulk processing, and your own eval runs (chapter 13). They stack: a cached prefix processed in a batch is a fraction of the headline price. Reach for these before you compromise on quality.

Latency is a different problem

Speed doesn't track cost. Two numbers matter: time to first token (how long before anything appears) and tokens per second (how fast it then streams). Because output is generated sequentially, output length drives latency more than input length, the opposite of cost, so "be concise" is a latency fix as well as a cost one. The techniques:

  • Stream the response, so the user sees words immediately; perceived latency drops even though total time is unchanged. This is the single biggest UX win.
  • Parallelise independent calls instead of chaining them (chapter 9's parallelisation pattern).
  • Use a smaller or faster model for latency-sensitive steps; the cascade helps here too, since most requests get the fast model.
  • Prompt caching cuts time to first token, not just cost, because the cached prefix isn't recomputed.
  • Do less sequentially: a long agent chain is slow by construction (chapter 9), so shortening it helps latency and reliability at once.

Budget every request

A non-deterministic system can run away, an agent loops, a retry storm hits, a prompt balloons, so cap every request: a maximum number of tokens, of model calls, of tool steps, and of dollars, after which it stops and falls back (chapter 14). This is the "cost ceiling per request" in this stage's deliverable, and it's what stands between you and a single pathological request, or a bad deploy, running up an unbounded bill. Track cost and latency per request in your telemetry (chapter 16), alert on the tail, and treat them as eval dimensions, so a model or prompt change that doubles cost is a regression your gate can see (chapter 13).

Common traps
  • Using the biggest model for everything, when most requests don't need it.
  • Optimising output length for cost while ignoring that input usually dominates the bill.
  • Routing to a cheaper model without an eval to confirm it's good enough.
  • No per-request budget, so one runaway request or loop is unbounded.
  • Treating latency as fixed, instead of streaming and parallelising.
Exercises
Exercise 15.1Find the biggest lever

A feature sends 8,000 input tokens (a fixed 6,000-token instruction set plus 2,000 of user content) and generates 500 output tokens, on the big model, a million times a day. Rank the options by savings: (a) switch 70% of traffic to a small model via a cascade; (b) cache the fixed instructions; (c) cut output to 300 tokens.

Show solution

Per request on the big model ($3 in / $15 out per M): input 8,000 × $3/M = $0.024; output 500 × $15/M = $0.0075; total ~$0.0315, so ~$31,500/day.

  • (b) Cache the 6,000 fixed tokens: they drop to 10% on repeat, saving 6,000 × $3/M × 0.9 ≈ $0.0162 per request, ~$16,200/day. Huge, and free in quality.
  • (a) Cascade 70% to a small model: those requests fall roughly tenfold in price; very large saving too, but it depends on the small model passing your eval on that slice.
  • (c) Cut output 500→300: saves 200 × $15/M = $0.003 per request, ~$3,000/day. Real, but the smallest of the three, and it also helps latency.

Caching and the cascade dwarf output trimming, because input dominates. Do the free one (caching) first, then the cascade with eval backing, then tune output.

Exercise 15.2Diagnose the latency

Users say a summariser "feels slow", though total time is 4 seconds for a 600-token summary. The call isn't streamed. What would you change, and what wouldn't help?

Show solution

Stream it. Four seconds staring at a spinner feels far worse than four seconds of text appearing as it's generated; streaming changes the perceived latency without changing the total. Beyond that, a 600-token output is inherently several seconds because generation is sequential, so if it must be faster, shorten the summary or use a faster model for this step. What won't help: optimising the input side (caching, fewer input tokens) barely moves latency here, because latency is dominated by generating 600 output tokens, not by reading the input. This is the mirror image of the cost lever.

Exercise 15.3Set the budgets

You're shipping an agent (chapter 9) that can call tools in a loop. Define the per-request budgets and what happens when each is hit.

Show solution
  • Max steps (tool-call iterations): stop and return the best answer so far, or fall back to a human, when exceeded, this also bounds the reliability tax of chapter 9.
  • Max tokens across the whole request: prune or summarise context (chapter 5) as it grows, and hard-stop at the cap.
  • Max cost in dollars: track running spend and abort to a fallback, so no single request can run up an unbounded bill.
  • Max wall-clock time: return a partial or fallback rather than leaving the user waiting indefinitely.

Each limit degrades to a safe fallback, not an exception, and each breach is logged and alerted, because hitting a budget is usually a sign the task was mis-scoped or something is looping.

Checklist
  • Do you send the fewest input tokens that do the job, and cache the stable prefix?
  • Are requests routed to the smallest model your eval says is good enough?
  • Do you use the batch API for offline work and evals?
  • Is the response streamed, and are independent calls parallelised?
  • Does every request have token, step, cost and time budgets with a safe fallback?

Chapter 16

Observability for non-deterministic systems

8 min read3 exercises

You can't reproduce a model's run, so the only way to understand what happened is to have captured it. Trace every request end to end, sample what you keep, let failures flow back into the eval set, and watch for the input and model drift that silently moves quality under you.

Why ordinary logging isn't enough

The Engineer's Watch covered logging, metrics and tracing for services. AI features add a twist that changes the emphasis: the system is non-deterministic, so "run it again and see" doesn't work, the second run is a different run. When a user reports a bad answer, you cannot reconstruct it from a stack trace; you can only inspect it if you recorded the whole thing at the time. So the bar is higher: capture, for every request, the input, the retrieved context, the exact prompt sent, the model and version and parameters, the raw output, every tool call and result, and the tokens, cost, latency and guardrail verdicts. That record is both your debugger and the raw material for new eval cases.

Trace the whole request

Structure the record as a trace of nested spans, one per step, the same model as distributed tracing, now standardised for AI by OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions and supported by tools such as Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix and Braintrust.

Rolled up, the trace shows at a glance that generation dominates both latency and cost while retrieval is a rounding error, which tells you where to optimise (chapter 15) and, when something's wrong, which span to open. In production you'd attach the actual prompt and output to the generate span, so a bad answer can be read, diffed and understood, not guessed at.

Sample, but always keep the failures

At scale you can't store every full trace, inputs and outputs are large, and may contain PII. Sample: keep a small random fraction of normal traffic for baselines, and keep everything that's interesting, errors, guardrail trips, low-confidence answers, user complaints, high cost or latency. The failures are the valuable ones, because each is a candidate eval case. And redact PII before it lands in your telemetry (chapter 14), with a retention policy, since a trace store is a pile of personal data like any other (The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 19).

Replay and feedback close the loop

Two things turn captured traces into improvement. Replay: re-run a stored request against a new prompt or model to see whether your fix actually fixes it, and to turn a production failure into an eval case, which is the flywheel of chapter 13. Feedback: capture the signals users already give, a thumbs-down, an edit to your draft, a regeneration, a follow-up that rephrases the same question, because these are free quality labels. A spike in regenerations on one feature is a quality alarm no technical metric would show. Fold both into the eval set so the system learns from its own production failures.

Watch for drift

Two things move under a live AI feature. Input drift: users start asking about things your eval set never covered, a new product, a seasonal topic, an incident. Model drift: the provider updates the model behind your pinned name, or you upgrade, and behaviour shifts. A cheap, standard detector is the population stability index, which measures how far a distribution has moved from a baseline:

A steady week scores near zero; a week where the "other" category surged scores 0.76, well past the 0.25 threshold, flagging that users are now asking things your system, and your eval set, weren't built for. The response is the loop again: investigate the new inputs, add them as eval cases, and improve coverage before quality quietly erodes. Apply the same check to output distributions (lengths, refusal rates, chosen categories) to catch a model update changing behaviour. And remember the point of all this is the business metric, resolved tickets, completed tasks, user satisfaction, not token counts; the telemetry exists to keep that number honest.

Common traps
  • Logging only the final output, so a bad answer can't be traced to its cause.
  • No way to replay a request, so you can't tell if a fix worked or build a case from a failure.
  • Ignoring user feedback signals that are free quality labels.
  • No drift detection, so a traffic shift or a model update erodes quality unseen.
  • Raw PII in traces, with no redaction or retention policy.
Exercises
Exercise 16.1What to capture

A user reports "the assistant gave me wrong refund information yesterday at about 3pm". With good observability, how do you investigate? List what you must have logged.

Show solution

You find the user's traces around that time and open the one for the refund question. To diagnose it you need: the exact input; the retrieved chunks and their scores (was the right policy retrieved? a chapter 7 question); the full prompt sent and the model version and parameters; the raw output; any tool calls and results; and the guardrail verdicts. From these you can localise the fault, retrieval missed the chunk, the chunk was wrong, or the model ignored it, and then replay the request against a fixed prompt to confirm the fix, and add it as an eval case so it can't regress. Without these logged, all you can do is guess, and you can't reproduce the run.

Exercise 16.2Design the sampling

You serve 5 million requests a day and can't store full traces for all of them. What sampling policy keeps costs down without going blind?

Show solution
  • Keep all the interesting ones: every error, guardrail trip, low-confidence or abstained answer, thumbs-down, high cost or latency, and anything a user flagged. These are rare and precious.
  • Sample a small random fraction of normal traffic (say 1%) for baselines and drift detection.
  • Always keep lightweight metadata (tokens, cost, latency, category, model version, guardrail result) for every request, even when you drop the full input/output, so your aggregates and drift metrics stay complete.
  • Redact PII on the way in and set a retention window.

The principle: cheap metadata for everything, full traces for a sample plus all failures.

Exercise 16.3Read the drift

Your output-length distribution has a PSI of 0.4 versus last month, and user thumbs-down are up, though no one changed the prompt. What likely happened, and what do you do?

Show solution

A large output-distribution shift with no prompt change points to model drift: the provider updated the model behind your pinned name, or your pin slipped to "latest" (chapter 13), and the new version is more verbose or differently behaved, which the rising thumbs-down confirms is hurting users. Steps: check whether the model version actually changed; run your eval suite against the current behaviour to quantify the regression; pin to a known-good version if the provider still offers it, or adapt the prompt and re-evaluate for the new one (chapter 13's migration); and add the newly-failing cases to the eval set. The drift metric is what turned "users seem less happy" into a specific, actionable cause.

Checklist
  • Do you capture the full trace, input, context, prompt, model version, output, tools, cost, for requests?
  • Can you replay a captured request against a new prompt or model?
  • Do failures and user-feedback signals flow back into the eval set?
  • Do you detect input and output drift, and alert on it?
  • Is PII redacted in telemetry, with a retention policy?

Chapter 17

Fine-tuning and distillation

8 min read3 exercises

Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour by training it on your examples. It's for form, not facts: style, format and consistency, never knowledge, which belongs in retrieval. Most teams never need it, and the one case that reliably pays off, distillation for cost, only does so at volume and only when an eval proves the smaller model is good enough.

The ladder: climb only as far as you must

There are four ways to adapt a model to your task, and they form a ladder you should climb one rung at a time: prompting (change the instructions), RAG (supply the knowledge), fine-tuning (change the behaviour), distillation (make it cheap). Each rung is more work, more maintenance and more commitment than the last, so you go up only when the rung below provably isn't enough, proof being your eval. A rule encodes the decision:

Changing, cited knowledge is a retrieval problem, so it stays at prompt + RAG. A strict house style with plenty of examples is a form problem, so it earns a fine-tune. A high-volume task the base model already handles is a cost problem, so it's a distillation candidate. And a task the base model already passes stops at prompting, the most common and most ignored answer. Climbing the ladder when you didn't need to is the usual mistake.

Fine-tuning is for form, not facts

This is the point teams most often get wrong, and it's worth stating flatly: fine-tuning does not reliably teach the model new facts. Train it on your company handbook and it learns the style of your handbook, not its contents, and will still confabulate specifics, now in your house voice. Knowledge that must be correct, current or cited belongs in retrieval (Part III). What fine-tuning is good at is shaping behaviour that examples in the prompt can't pin down across the whole distribution: a consistent tone and format, a narrow classification done the same way every time, a particular refusal style, a structured output a schema can't fully express. Use it when prompting and RAG leave a gap in how the model responds, not in what it knows.

When you do fine-tune, three preconditions matter: a stable task (if it changes monthly, you'll retrain monthly), a real eval (fine-tuning without one is flying blind, you can't tell if it helped or caused catastrophic forgetting of general ability), and enough in-distribution examples, 500 is a rough floor, of the quality you want out. Technically, reach for LoRA or QLoRA: these train small "adapter" weights on top of a frozen base model, cheaply, on a single GPU, without touching or needing to store the full model. Full fine-tuning is rarely the right call in 2026. Preference methods like DPO tune toward chosen-over-rejected examples when what you're shaping is a judgment call rather than a format.

Distillation: the case that pays

The strongest reason to fine-tune is cost, not capability. Distillation uses a frontier model to generate high-quality outputs for your task, then fine-tunes a small, cheap model on those outputs, so you pay the frontier price once, to create training data, and serve forever on something a fraction of the cost and faster. The economics are stark at volume:

A one-off cost of a few hundred dollars to label data and train an adapter breaks even in 45 days at a thousand requests a day, and in hours at a hundred thousand, cutting the monthly serving bill from $36,000 to $1,800. The pattern is "teacher labels, student serves", and it's the most reliable win in this chapter, with one hard condition: the small model must pass your eval on the task. Distillation trades generality for a cheap specialist, so it only works when the task is narrow enough that a specialist suffices, which, again, only the eval can tell you.

What fine-tuning costs you

Before you climb, count the ongoing price, which is why RAG and prompting are preferred when they'll do. A fine-tuned model is a data pipeline you now maintain and a model you must re-tune on every base-model upgrade, so you've traded the provider's free improvements for a model frozen at your last training run. It can regress general ability while gaining your narrow skill. And it bakes in whatever was in the training data, including its mistakes and biases (chapter 20), far less visibly than a prompt you can read. None of this is a reason never to fine-tune; it's a reason to be sure the rungs below genuinely don't suffice, and to keep the eval running afterwards, because a fine-tune is a bet that only measurement can settle.

Common traps
  • Fine-tuning to add knowledge, which it doesn't reliably do, use RAG.
  • Fine-tuning before trying prompting and RAG, and before having an eval to judge it.
  • Distilling a task the small model can't actually handle, saving money by shipping worse answers.
  • Forgetting the maintenance cost: re-tuning on every model upgrade, a data pipeline to keep.
  • Full fine-tuning where a cheap LoRA adapter would do.
Exercises
Exercise 17.1Climb the ladder

For each, which rung (prompt, RAG, fine-tune, distill) and why?

  1. The assistant should always answer in your brand's distinctive terse style; prompting with examples gets it right 70% of the time.
  2. It must answer policy questions correctly from a wiki that changes weekly.
  3. It classifies 2 million support messages a day into 12 intents; the frontier model is accurate but the bill is huge.
  4. It needs to know the capital of France.
Show solution
  1. Fine-tune. It's a form problem that prompting can't fully pin; collect examples of the style and tune (with an eval to confirm it beats 70% without regressing elsewhere).
  2. RAG. It's knowledge, and it changes weekly, exactly what fine-tuning can't keep up with and retrieval handles by updating documents.
  3. Distill. High volume, a narrow task the frontier model already does well: label a dataset with the frontier model, fine-tune a small model, serve cheaply, if it passes the eval on all 12 intents.
  4. Prompt, or rather nothing, the base model already knows it. Don't climb the ladder at all.
Exercise 17.2Do the distillation sum

Using the chapter's numbers (frontier $0.012/req, small $0.0006/req, one-off $520), at what daily volume does distillation break even within 30 days? Below that, what would you do instead?

Show solution

Daily saving per request is $0.012 − $0.0006 = $0.0114. To recoup $520 in 30 days you need $520 / 30 ≈ $17.3/day of saving, which is 17.3 / 0.0114 ≈ 1,520 requests/day. Below roughly that volume, the one-off cost and the ongoing maintenance aren't worth it: stay on the frontier model with prompting, and reach for cheaper wins first, a cascade to a (non-fine-tuned) smaller model on easy requests, prompt caching, and the batch API (chapter 15), none of which carry a training pipeline to maintain.

Exercise 17.3The fine-tune that didn't help

A team fine-tuned a model on 5,000 support transcripts hoping it would answer product questions more accurately. Accuracy didn't improve, and it now sometimes states old prices confidently. What happened, and what should they do?

Show solution

They used fine-tuning to inject knowledge, which it doesn't reliably do: the model absorbed the style of the transcripts and some stale facts from them, so it now confabulates outdated prices in a convincing support voice, worse than before. The fix is to move knowledge to RAG: retrieve current product and pricing data and have the model answer from it with citations (Part III). If they also want the support tone, that's the legitimate use of the fine-tune, keep it for form, but let retrieval supply the facts, and measure both with the eval. This is the single most common fine-tuning mistake.

Checklist
  • Have prompting and RAG been tried, and found genuinely insufficient, first?
  • Are you fine-tuning for form and behaviour, with knowledge left to retrieval?
  • Do you have a stable task, a real eval, and enough in-distribution examples?
  • For cost-driven cases, does distillation break even at your volume, with the small model passing the eval?
  • Have you budgeted the ongoing cost of re-tuning on every model upgrade?

Part VI

Judgment

Three chapters on the judgment that surrounds the engineering: enough classical machine learning to be literate and to know when not to use a language model at all, how to work with coding agents without losing ownership of your code, and the ethics that are also engineering decisions.

Chapter 18

Classical machine learning literacy

8 min read3 exercises

You don't need to train neural networks to build with foundation models, but you need the literacy: train and test splits, overfitting, baselines, the metrics from chapter 11. These ideas underpin evaluation, and they tell you the thing a language model enthusiast most needs to hear, that for many tasks a boring classical model is cheaper, faster, and better.

Why a builder needs this

Three reasons to carry a little classical machine learning. First, the eval concepts are classical ML: train/test splits, overfitting, precision and recall, baselines, you've been using them since chapter 10, and understanding them makes your evals sharper. Second, literacy: you'll work with data scientists and read model cards, and the vocabulary is shared. Third, and most useful, knowing when not to reach for an LLM: a large fraction of "AI" problems are better solved by a classical model that's cheaper, faster, interpretable and more reliable, and recognising those saves you from bringing a language model to a logistic-regression fight.

Train, test, and the cardinal sin

The foundational discipline is splitting your data: train the model on one part, and measure it on a held-out test part it never saw. Evaluating on data the model trained on tells you how well it memorised, not how well it generalises, which is the only thing that matters in production. (A three-way split adds a validation set for tuning choices, keeping the test set pristine for a final, honest number.) This is exactly the eval discipline of chapter 11, the held-out set you don't tune against, and the warning there about overfitting your eval is the same warning in a new guise.

Overfitting, underfitting, and baselines

A model overfits when it learns the noise in the training data instead of the signal, acing the training set and failing on new data; it underfits when it's too simple to capture the real pattern. You can watch it happen:

The true relationship is a line. A degree-1 fit recovers it and generalises best (test MSE 1.83). A degree-9 polynomial bends through every training point, driving train error almost to zero (0.04) while test error balloons to 12.47, it memorised the noise. And every model is measured against a baseline, here "predict the mean", which scores 26.47: a model that can't beat the dumbest possible predictor is worthless, and you'd be surprised how often an elaborate system fails that bar. Always compute the baseline first. For an LLM feature, the baseline might be a keyword rule or a majority-class guess; if the model barely beats it, the model isn't earning its cost.

When a classical model wins

Language models are general, which makes them a poor default for narrow, well-defined problems. Reach for classical machine learning, or no learning at all, when:

  • The data is tabular or structured. Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM) and logistic regression beat LLMs on rows-and-columns prediction, churn, fraud, pricing, and run in microseconds.
  • The task is narrow and you have labels. A text classifier trained on ten thousand labelled examples is cheaper, faster and often more accurate than prompting a general model for the same label, and it doesn't hallucinate.
  • You need speed, low cost, or determinism at scale. A classical model serves millions of predictions for the price of one LLM call, repeatably.
  • You need interpretability. A regression's coefficients explain themselves to a regulator; a model's hidden state doesn't.
  • A rule or heuristic suffices. Sometimes the right amount of machine learning is none: a regex, a lookup table, a threshold. Don't let "AI" talk you out of the simple answer.

The flip side defines the LLM's home turf: unstructured language, open-ended generation, tasks with no training data, and problems where the generality is the point. A mature system often combines them, a cheap classifier routes or filters, and the LLM handles the genuinely language-shaped part. Karpathy's framing holds: "Software 1.0" (code), "2.0" (trained models) and "3.0" (prompted models) are three tools, and good engineering picks the right one per sub-problem rather than forcing everything through the newest.

Common traps
  • Evaluating on training data, and mistaking memorisation for skill.
  • No baseline, so you can't tell whether the model adds anything.
  • Reaching for an LLM on tabular data, where trees or regression win on every axis.
  • Confusing low training error with a good model, the signature of overfitting.
  • Using a language model where a rule or lookup would do, paying for generality you don't need.
Exercises
Exercise 18.1Read the curve

In the example, degree 1 beats degree 3 on test error (1.83 vs 3.04) even though degree 3 is more flexible. Why? And what would you expect at degree 15?

Show solution

The true relationship is a line (degree 1), so the extra flexibility of degree 3 buys nothing but a chance to chase noise, which it does, raising test error. Degree 1 matches the underlying form, so it generalises best, this is choosing a model complexity that matches the problem, not maximising flexibility. At degree 15 (with only ~11 training points) the polynomial would interpolate the training data almost exactly, train error near zero, and test error would be far worse still, wild oscillations between the points. More capacity is not better; the right capacity is.

Exercise 18.2LLM or classical?

For each, choose a language model, a classical ML model, or a plain rule, and say why.

  1. Predict which customers will churn next month, from 40 account metrics.
  2. Answer open-ended questions about a product from its documentation.
  3. Flag transactions over $10,000 from outside the user's usual country.
  4. Route 2 million support emails a day to one of 15 teams.
Show solution
  1. Classical (gradient-boosted trees). Tabular features, a clear label, needs speed and interpretability, an LLM would be worse and far costlier.
  2. LLM with RAG. Unstructured language and open-ended generation: its home turf.
  3. A rule. Two thresholds; no learning needed. Don't over-engineer.
  4. Probably classical (a trained text classifier), given the volume, the fixed label set and the cost of 2M LLM calls, though you might distil an LLM into that classifier (chapter 17). Validate with the same precision/recall per team as any eval.
Exercise 18.3Set the baseline

You're about to build an LLM feature that categorises news articles into 8 topics. Before writing any prompt, what baselines would you establish, and how would they shape the decision?

Show solution
  • Majority class: always predict the most common topic, its accuracy is the floor any model must clear.
  • Keyword rules: a handful of per-topic keyword matchers, cheap and surprisingly strong on news.
  • A classical classifier: TF-IDF features into logistic regression, trained on a few thousand labelled articles, minutes to build, often very competitive.

Then measure the LLM against all three on a held-out test set, with per-topic precision and recall (chapter 11). If the LLM only ties the keyword rules or the classifier, it's not worth its cost and latency, use the classical model. If it clearly wins on the hard, ambiguous articles, it earns its place, perhaps as the escalation tier of a cascade (chapter 15). The baseline turns "should we use an LLM here?" from a hunch into a measurement.

Checklist
  • Do you always measure on held-out data the model never saw?
  • Do you compute a dumb baseline before judging any model?
  • Can you recognise overfitting (great train score, poor test score)?
  • Do you consider a classical model or a rule before defaulting to an LLM?
  • For narrow, structured, high-volume tasks, have you checked whether an LLM is even the right tool?

Chapter 19

Working with coding agents

7 min read3 exercises

A coding agent is the same kind of component as everything else in this book: fluent, fast, and confidently wrong in ways you can't see by reading. So treat it the same way. Specify precisely, keep the spec and the tests as the thing you own, review every diff, and never ship a line you can't explain.

The same component, pointed at your codebase

You've spent this whole volume learning to build on a model that's brilliant and unreliable in uneven patches. A coding agent is that model, with tools, aimed at your repository, so everything you know applies: it hallucinates (an API that doesn't exist, a plausible but wrong fix), it has jagged intelligence (it writes a subtle concurrency fix, then botches a date comparison), and its confidence is no evidence of correctness. The Syllabus puts the rule plainly: a coding agent is leverage on a foundation and a liability without one, and the discipline that keeps you honest is that you must be able to explain every line you ship. This chapter applies the book's own methods, spec, eval, review, ownership, to the agent writing your code.

The spec and the tests are what you own

When an agent writes the implementation, the artifact you author and keep is the specification and the tests. They are the eval for code: the executable statement of what "working" means, which outlives any particular implementation. Write them first, or at least alongside, because a clear spec is both how you get good output from the agent and how you catch bad output:

The agent's first draft, qty * price, is exactly what a plausible description produces, and it passes the happy-path cases, so it reads as correct. The spec's edge cases, the per-order cap and the rejection of negative inputs, fail it, 4 of 7, surfacing the requirements that review by eye would have waved through. This is the chapter 13 gate again: the tests, not your confidence or the agent's, decide whether the code is right. Write the hard cases down, because those are the ones the agent, and you, will otherwise miss.

Review agent code harder, not softer

It's tempting to skim a diff that looks clean and compiles. Resist it, as The Engineer's Craft, chapter 13, argued about reviewing assistant-written code: review it at least as carefully as a new colleague's, because the agent optimises for plausible, not correct, and plausible code passes a glance. Specifically: check the edge cases and error paths the happy path hides; check that it does what you asked and nothing more (agents add unrequested helpers, dependencies and config); check security, an agent will cheerfully write the SQL-injectable query or the over-broad permission (The Engineer's Citadel); and run it, don't just read it. The firmest rule, and the one that scales: don't approve what you can't explain. If you can't say why a line is there and what it does, it isn't ready, whoever typed it.

Keep ownership, and scope the agent

You are accountable for the code you merge; "the agent wrote it" is no more a defence than "the chatbot said it" was for Air Canada. Two practices keep ownership real. Small, reviewable diffs: a hundred-line change you understand beats a thousand-line one you skim, so steer the agent toward incremental, test-backed steps rather than a grand generation. And scope its powers like any agent (chapter 9, Citadel chapter 20): a coding agent with unrestricted access to run commands, touch production, or push to main is the Replit database deletion waiting to happen, where an agent ran destructive commands during a code freeze. Give it a sandbox, keep humans on the irreversible actions (merging, deploying, migrations), and require the test suite to pass before anything lands.

The skill that's actually changing

The leverage is real: agents genuinely accelerate the typing, the boilerplate, the unfamiliar API, the first draft. What they shift is where your skill is spent, from producing code to specifying it precisely, reviewing it critically, and testing it thoroughly, the three things this book has been about for a different kind of model. An engineer who can write a sharp spec, read a diff with suspicion, and design the test that catches the edge case is more valuable with agents, not less. One who approves fluent code they don't understand has automated the production of liabilities. The rule from the start of the Syllabus is the whole of it: let the assistant write code only after you can read it.

Common traps
  • Approving code you can't explain because it looks clean and compiles.
  • No tests, so the agent's plausible-but-wrong edge cases ship.
  • Huge diffs skimmed rather than reviewed.
  • An agent with unscoped power to run commands, touch production, or merge.
  • Trusting the agent's confidence, the same mistake as trusting any model's fluency.
Exercises
Exercise 19.1Write the spec first

You're about to ask an agent to implement "parse a user's date-of-birth from free text". Before it writes anything, list the test cases you'd put in the spec.

Show solution

The value is in the cases the agent won't volunteer: multiple formats (ISO, DD/MM/YYYY, MM/DD/YYYY and the ambiguity between them, written months); two-digit years; impossible dates (31 February, month 13); future dates and implausibly old ones; missing or partial dates; non-date text; and the "can't parse" path that must return a clear "not found" rather than guessing (chapter 4). You'd also decide the output type (a date object, not a string) and the locale assumption. Writing these down is most of the engineering; the implementation is comparatively easy, and now the agent's output is judged against your spec, not your optimism.

Exercise 19.2Review the diff

An agent's diff adds the feature you asked for, and also adds a new third-party dependency, a broadened database query "for flexibility", and a // TODO: add auth later. It passes the tests. Do you merge? What do you do?

Show solution

No. Passing tests is necessary, not sufficient, and this diff does more than you asked, the classic agent over-reach. The new dependency is a supply-chain decision (Citadel chapter 14) that needs justifying, not slipping in. The broadened query is a likely security and correctness regression (it may now return rows it shouldn't, chapter on access control) and "for flexibility" is not a reason. The auth TODO is a security hole shipped with a comment on it. Send it back: scope the change to exactly what was asked, drop or justify the dependency, tighten the query, and either add auth now or don't touch that path. The test suite didn't catch these because they aren't about the happy path, which is exactly why human review of the diff is irreplaceable.

Exercise 19.3Scope the agent

Your team wants to run a coding agent that can read the repo, run the test suite, and open pull requests automatically. What powers do you grant, and what do you gate?

Show solution
  • Grant freely (reversible, sandboxed): read the repo, run tests and linters in an isolated environment, open a draft pull request.
  • Gate on a human: merging to main, deploying, running database migrations, touching production data or secrets, adding dependencies, anything the Replit incident is a warning about.
  • Deny or sandbox: arbitrary shell against production, network egress beyond what a build needs (Citadel chapter 6), write access to anything outside its working branch.
  • Require: the test suite and CI eval (chapter 13) pass before a human reviews, and a human reviews before anything merges.

The principle is the agent chapter's: automate the reversible, gate the irreversible, and keep the blast radius small, so even a confidently wrong agent can't do lasting harm.

Checklist
  • Do you write the spec and tests, and treat them as the thing you own?
  • Do you review agent diffs at least as carefully as a colleague's?
  • Can you explain every line before you approve it?
  • Are diffs small enough to actually review?
  • Is the agent sandboxed, with humans gating merges, deploys and migrations?

Chapter 20

The ethics that are also engineering

8 min read3 exercises

The ethical questions about an AI feature, is it fair, does it credit its sources, do people know they're talking to a machine, did you have the right to this data, are not separate from the engineering. Each is a property you can measure and build for, with the same discipline as every other chapter. Ethics you can't measure is a press release; ethics you can is a test in CI.

Four questions, all measurable

The Syllabus lists the ethics of this stage as bias, attribution, disclosure and informed consent, and groups them with the engineering for a reason: each is a decision you implement, not a value you profess. Treat them as you've treated everything else in this volume, as something to measure, gate and monitor, and they stop being vague obligations and become part of your eval.

Bias: measure it, or you're guessing

A model learns from data, including the data's skews, and your own data adds more, so an AI feature can work well on average and badly for a particular group. "Is it fair?" is not a feeling; it's the per-slice measurement of chapter 11, pointed at the groups a mistake would harm:

The headline accuracy, 88%, looks fine, and would pass a careless eval. Slice the same errors by group and a different picture appears: group B's innocent users are wrongly flagged nine times as often as group A's. That disparate false-positive rate is a real harm, people inconvenienced, suspected, or denied, concentrated on one group, and the only reason you can see it is that you measured per slice. You can't fix what you don't measure, so the engineering obligation is concrete: build fairness slices into the eval (chapter 11), gate on them in CI (chapter 13), and document the model's known limitations and the groups it serves worse. Which disparities matter, and what to do about them, is a judgment that needs more than engineers in the room; measuring them is the part you own.

Attribution: restore the provenance the model strips

A model is a provenance launderer: it emits fluent text with no trace of where the knowledge came from, and presenting that as original, authoritative, or the model's own is a problem both ethical and practical. The engineering answer is grounding and citation (Part III): retrieve from known sources and cite them, so a claim can be checked and its author credited. Beyond citations, respect the licensing of what the model reproduces, code under a licence, text under copyright, and don't let a generative step quietly strip the attribution that the source required. The Mata v. Avianca lawyers' deeper error wasn't just that the cases were fake; it was treating the model's unsourced output as authoritative. Cite, link, and let the user verify.

Disclosure: don't pretend it isn't AI

People are entitled to know when they're interacting with a machine or reading machine-generated content, and increasingly the law agrees: the EU AI Act, among others, requires that users be told when they're talking to an AI system and that AI-generated content be marked. Beyond compliance, it's a matter of not deceiving, a chatbot that implies it's a human, or an AI report passed off as fully human-authored (the Deloitte case), breaks trust when discovered, which it will be. Disclose that it's AI, disclose material limitations, and don't let the interface imply a competence or a humanity the system lacks. This connects to the whole volume's refrain: you own the output, so you own how it's represented.

Informed consent: the right to the data

AI features run on data, and having access to data is not the same as having the right to use it this way. The privacy engineering of The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 19, applies in full: minimise what you collect, use it only for the purpose the person agreed to, and don't feed customer data to a model, or into training, without a lawful basis and a clear disclosure. Two AI-specific traps: anything you send to a model provider leaves your systems, so redact PII first (chapter 14) and know the provider's data-retention and training terms; and fine-tuning or building an eval set on user data is a use of that data that needs consent, not a technicality. Consent is an engineering requirement because it determines what your pipeline is allowed to do.

The discipline is the ethics

Step back, and the ethics of this chapter turn out to be the same practice as the rest of the volume. Measuring bias is slicing your eval. Attribution is grounding and citation. Disclosure is honesty about a system you own. Consent is privacy built into the data pipeline. The thread running through all twenty chapters is that a language model is a powerful, unreliable component, and engineering it well means refusing to trust its fluency, measuring what it actually does, and taking responsibility for the result, to your users, and to the people its outputs affect. That responsibility is the job. The eval is how you meet it.

Common traps
  • Reporting only aggregate accuracy, so a harm concentrated on one group is invisible.
  • Passing off unsourced model output as authoritative, with nothing to verify or credit.
  • Interfaces that imply a human or a competence the system doesn't have.
  • Sending user data to a provider, or training on it, without consent or redaction.
  • Treating ethics as a policy document rather than slices, gates and disclosures in the product.
Exercises
Exercise 20.1Find the hidden harm

A resume-screening feature reports 91% agreement with past hiring decisions, and the team wants to ship. What would you measure first, and why is 91% not enough?

Show solution

Two problems. First, agreeing with past decisions means it learned to reproduce past bias, so a high agreement number can be a measure of how faithfully it copies discrimination, the target is itself suspect. Second, 91% overall says nothing about whom it rejects: slice selection rates and error rates by gender, ethnicity, age and any protected attribute, as in the chapter's example, and look for disparate impact. You'd also check what features it keys on (proxies for protected attributes, like postcode or school). The right first step is per-group measurement against a fair target, not aggregate agreement with a biased history, and in many places this is also a legal requirement, not only an ethical one.

Exercise 20.2Design the disclosures

You're shipping an AI assistant on a public website that answers questions and can draft emails for users. List the disclosures and consents you'd build in.

Show solution
  • It's AI: make clear at the start of the interaction that it's an automated assistant, not a human agent.
  • Limitations: note that it can be wrong and how to reach a human or verify, especially for anything consequential (the Air Canada lesson).
  • Attribution: cite the sources behind factual answers so users can check them.
  • Data use: tell users what happens to what they type, that it may go to a model provider, retention, and whether it's used to improve the service, with a real choice where consent is required.
  • Generated content: if it drafts an email the user sends, that's the user's to review and own; don't auto-send on their behalf without confirmation (chapter 14).
Exercise 20.3Make the ethics testable

Turn "our assistant should be fair, honest and respect privacy" into things your eval and CI can actually check.

Show solution
  • Fair: eval slices per protected group with error-rate parity thresholds (chapter 11), gated in CI (chapter 13); a critical case set that must never regress on the worst-served group.
  • Honest: faithfulness checks that every claim is grounded in a cited source (chapter 7); a disclosure-present check in the UI; an eval case that the assistant identifies itself as AI when asked.
  • Privacy: an automated check that PII is redacted before egress to the provider and before logging (chapter 14); tests that the assistant refuses to reveal other users' data; a data-retention job with tests.

Each vague value becomes a slice, a gate or a check, which is the chapter's whole point: ethics you can measure is engineering, and this volume has been about measuring.

Checklist
  • Do your evals slice error rates by the groups a mistake would harm?
  • Does the system cite its sources so claims can be checked and credited?
  • Are users told they're interacting with AI, and told its limitations?
  • Is user data redacted, consented, and used only as agreed, including for evals and fine-tuning?
  • Are these turned into slices, gates and checks, not just a policy page?

The twenty rules

One per chapter, each linked back to it. Read them before you ship an AI feature, and against every change that touches a prompt, a model, retrieval or an eval.

  1. Never trust fluency as a sign of truth; the model predicts plausible tokens, not correct ones.
  2. Search by meaning with embeddings, but use keywords for exact IDs and never expect cosine to respect negation.
  3. Treat the prompt as versioned, testable code, and decompose a hard task rather than over-instructing one call.
  4. Use the strongest schema enforcement your provider offers, validate the values, and let the model answer "unknown".
  5. Send the least context that does the job, ordered stable-to-volatile so the prefix caches, with the key material at the ends.
  6. Ground answers in retrieved, cited facts; chunk on real boundaries with overlap and metadata.
  7. Run hybrid search, rerank to a few, and measure retrieval and faithfulness separately from the answer.
  8. Give the model narrow, validated tools, treat their output as untrusted, and gate every irreversible action.
  9. Prefer a single call or a fixed workflow; reach for an agent only when the path is unknowable, then bound and gate it.
  10. Judge every change by an eval on your own data, not by eye and not by a public benchmark.
  11. Cover the edge, adversarial and no-answer cases, pick the metric that matches the cost of being wrong, and slice it.
  12. Judge open-ended output with a rubric, cancel the judge's biases, and calibrate it against humans before trusting it.
  13. Run the eval in CI, block real regressions while tolerating noise, pin the model version, and grow the set from failures.
  14. Check input and output, redact PII, enforce safety by limiting capability, and keep a human gate and a fallback.
  15. Send fewer input tokens, use the smallest model your eval allows, cache and batch, stream, and budget every request.
  16. Capture full traces you can replay, feed failures and feedback back into the eval, and watch for drift.
  17. Climb prompt, RAG, fine-tune, distill only as far as needed; fine-tune for form, keep knowledge in retrieval.
  18. Measure on held-out data against a baseline, watch for overfitting, and use a classical model or a rule when it wins.
  19. Own the spec and the tests, review every agent diff, explain every line, and sandbox the agent's powers.
  20. Make fairness, attribution, disclosure and consent measurable slices, gates and checks, not a policy page.

Companion volume · Stage 06 of The Engineer's Syllabus

The Engineer's Exchange

An exchange is where lines meet and messages are routed: the telephone exchange that connected one caller to another, the internet exchange where networks hand traffic across, and the request-and-response exchange behind every page you load. Almost everything you build is reached over a network, and almost every mysterious slowness lives in it. This volume follows that message from the HTTP you write, down through TCP and IP to the wire, and back up again.

Chapters20
Code examples23
Exercises60
Stage budget120 h

How to use this volume

The chapters follow the shape of the rest of the series: the idea in one sentence, worked examples, the traps, then exercises with folded solutions, a checklist and further reading. Networking rewards doing over reading, so run the examples, point the tools at real servers, and watch the packets.

We go top-down. The classic networking course teaches the wire first and the web last; this one, like Kurose and Ross, starts where your work actually touches the network, HTTP, and descends: the web, then transport (TCP and UDP), then addressing (IP), then naming (DNS), then delivery at scale, then how to debug it all. The layer you'll meet first in your career is the layer we meet first here. The one prerequisite is a little computer architecture (stage 04): what a process, a port and a buffer are.

The examples use the real network, or stand in for it deterministically. Where an example can run against your own machine, over real sockets, with ipaddress, with a local HTTP server, it does, and it was executed before publication. Where it would depend on a live remote host (a real DNS answer, a real traceroute), it's shown as captured output and marked illustrative, because that output changes by the hour and your network isn't ours. Everything you can reproduce, you should.

Tools and numbers age; the shape doesn't. The adoption percentages, the fastest resolver, the default congestion-control algorithm, these are late-2026 snapshots that will drift, and they're here to show you how to find today's answer, not to memorise. What lasts is the model: the layers, the round trip, the handshake, the name lookup. The stage's deliverable is the real test: write an HTTP/1.1 server directly on TCP sockets, handling keep-alive, chunked encoding and concurrent connections, with no framework, then implement a working TCP stack in the CS 144 labs. Build the thing, and the layers stop being a diagram.

The one question

When something is slow or broken over a network, the instinct is to blame your code. Usually your code is fine and the network is doing something you didn't picture, because you pictured it as instant and direct, and it is neither.

So the question to ask of any networked operation, before you profile a single function, is: how many round trips does this take, and how far does each one travel? A round trip to a server across an ocean is 150 milliseconds no matter how fast your code is, and most mysterious latency turns out to be round trips you didn't know you were making, DNS lookups, TLS handshakes, redirects, chatty APIs, across distances light itself takes real time to cross. Learn to see the journey, and the network stops being magic.

Part I

The web

Five chapters on the layer you actually touch. We start, as the best networking course does, at the top: the layered model and how a request is wrapped for its journey, then URLs, then HTTP in depth, its caching and state, and the newer versions that make it fast.

Chapter 01

The network, top-down

8 min read3 exercises

The internet is built in layers, each solving one problem and handing the rest to the layer below. Your code writes at the top, in HTTP; by the time your message reaches the wire it has been wrapped four times over, and on the way it is read only by the layers that need it. Understand the layers and the journey, and the network stops being a black box.

Why layers

Getting a message from a program on your laptop to a program in a data centre on another continent is an enormous problem, so the internet splits it into independent sub-problems and stacks the solutions. The application layer decides what to say (HTTP, the request for a page). The transport layer gets that message to the right program on the far host and, with TCP, makes sure it arrives complete and in order. The network layer (IP) gets a packet to the right host, hop by hop, across any number of networks. The link layer moves bits across a single stretch of wire or radio to the next device. Each layer is a contract: it offers a service to the layer above and relies on the one below, so you can reason about HTTP without thinking about voltages, and swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet without changing a line of your app.

This is the TCP/IP model, four layers. You'll also hear the older seven-layer OSI model, which is mostly useful now as vocabulary: when someone says "a layer 7 load balancer" they mean it understands HTTP, and "layer 4" means it works at TCP. We'll use the four-layer model and borrow the numbers where they're handy.

Encapsulation: envelopes inside envelopes

A message doesn't move down the stack unchanged; each layer wraps it in a header of its own, like putting a letter in an envelope, then that envelope in a bigger one. On the far side the process reverses, each layer reads and strips its own header and hands the rest up. Here is the wrapping, with the real header sizes:

Two lessons fall out of the numbers. A layer reads only its own header: a router looks at the IP header to decide where to forward the packet and never opens the TCP or HTTP inside, which is both an efficiency and a privacy property (and why TLS, chapter 6, can hide everything above IP). And headers have a fixed cost, 54 bytes here, so carrying a single byte is 98% overhead while a full 1460-byte segment is only 3.6%: this is why chatty, tiny messages waste the network and why batching helps, a theme that returns in every later chapter.

The journey of a request

Follow one HTTP request. Your code hands HTTP to the transport layer, which splits it into segments and adds a TCP header with source and destination ports (so the far host knows which program the data is for) and sequence numbers (so it can be reassembled in order). Each segment goes to IP, which wraps it in a packet with source and destination IP addresses and hands it to the link layer, which frames it for the first hop. Then it travels: across your Wi-Fi to your router, which forwards it toward its destination; through your ISP; across the internet's backbone, router to router, each one reading the IP header, deciding the next hop, and passing it on; until it reaches the server's network, its host, and finally, unwrapped layer by layer, the server program. The reply makes the same trip in reverse. The whole round trip is what chapter 16 teaches you to count, because its duration is set by physics, not by your code.

The ideas that shaped it

  • Packet switching. The internet doesn't reserve a dedicated line for your conversation the way old telephone networks did; it chops data into packets that share links with everyone else's, each routed independently. That's why the internet is cheap and resilient (a packet routes around a failure) and also why latency varies (your packet waits in queues behind others).
  • The end-to-end principle. Keep the network in the middle simple and fast, and put the intelligence, reliability, ordering, encryption, at the endpoints. It's why IP itself makes no promises (a packet may be lost, duplicated or reordered) and TCP builds reliability on top, at the ends. This principle explains more design decisions in this volume than any other.
  • Addresses at every layer. A thing has a different name at each layer: a human-friendly hostname at the application layer (resolved by DNS, chapter 15), an IP address at the network layer (chapter 13), a port at the transport layer, and a hardware MAC address at the link layer. Confusing which name lives where is the source of many networking muddles.
Common traps
  • Imagining the network as instant and direct. It's a series of hops across real distance, each adding delay.
  • Mixing up the addresses: a port is not an IP, a hostname is not an IP, a MAC is not routable across the internet.
  • Thinking routers understand your request. They read the IP header and forward; the meaning lives at the ends.
  • Ignoring header overhead, and sending many tiny packets where a few full ones would do.
  • Treating the layers as leaky-free. They abstract, but performance problems cross them, which is why you learn all of them.
Exercises
Exercise 1.1Place the responsibility

Which layer handles each of these, and why?

  1. Making sure the bytes arrive in the order they were sent.
  2. Choosing which cable or radio to send the next hop over.
  3. Deciding which running program on the server receives the data.
  4. Finding a route from your city to a server in another country.
Show solution
  1. Transport (TCP). IP delivers packets that may arrive out of order; TCP's sequence numbers restore order at the receiving end (chapter 9).
  2. Link. It moves a frame across one physical segment to the next device; it has no idea about the end-to-end path.
  3. Transport, via the port number. The IP address gets the packet to the host; the port gets it to the right program (a web server on 443, say).
  4. Network (IP), through routing (chapter 14). Each router along the way makes a local next-hop decision based on the destination IP.
Exercise 1.2Do the overhead arithmetic

Using the chapter's header sizes (TCP 20, IP 20, Ethernet 14), a voice-chat app sends 20-byte audio samples, one per packet, 50 times a second. How much of the bandwidth is headers? What would you change?

Show solution

Each packet carries 20 bytes of audio under 54 bytes of headers, so 54 / 74 ≈ 73% of every packet is overhead, and at 50 packets a second you're paying that 73% tax constantly. (Real voice adds a UDP+RTP header too, making it worse.) The fix is to send fewer, larger packets, bundle several audio samples per packet, trading a little latency for much less overhead, which is exactly the trade every real-time codec tunes. It's also why protocols like QUIC work hard to shrink headers. The deeper point: on the network, the number of packets often matters as much as the number of bytes.

Exercise 1.3Trace the layers

You load a web page and it's slow. A colleague says "the server must be slow". Using the layered model, list four other places the delay could be, one per layer or hop.

Show solution
  • Application: a DNS lookup to resolve the hostname before anything else happens (chapter 15), or a chain of redirects.
  • Transport: the TCP handshake and TLS handshake, two or more round trips before the first byte of the page (chapters 6, 9), or packet loss triggering retransmission.
  • Network: a long path, many hops, or congestion queueing your packets, which a traceroute would show (chapter 19).
  • Link / last mile: a slow or lossy Wi-Fi link, or a congested home connection.

"The server is slow" is one hypothesis out of many, and usually not the right one. The rest of this volume is about telling them apart.

Checklist
  • Can you name the four layers and what each is responsible for?
  • Do you understand encapsulation, each layer wrapping the one above?
  • Do you know which address lives at which layer (hostname, IP, port, MAC)?
  • Can you explain why routers don't read your HTTP?
  • When something's slow, do you think in terms of the whole journey, not just the server?

Chapter 02

URLs and the web model

6 min read3 exercises

The web is a simple idea: every resource has an address, you fetch it by that address over HTTP, and resources link to each other. The address is the URL, and reading one correctly, its scheme, its host and port, its path and query, and knowing what an origin is, is the foundation of everything from routing to security.

Three inventions

Tim Berners-Lee's web rests on three things that still define it: a way to name any resource (the URL), a way to fetch it (HTTP, chapter 3), and a way to link resources into a web (hypertext). This chapter is about the first, because the name comes before the fetch, and because a surprising amount of networking and security is really about reading a URL correctly. The model is deliberately simple: a client asks for the resource at a URL, a server returns a representation of it, and that's a complete interaction. The resource might be a file, a database row rendered as JSON, or something computed on the spot; the URL names it without saying how it's produced.

Anatomy of a URL

Each part answers a different question, and they nest from general to specific:

A few parts repay attention. The fragment (#reviews) is handled entirely by the browser and never sent to the server, which is why single-page apps once used it for routing and why you can't read it in server logs. The query carries parameters, but it's part of the URL, so it ends up in logs, history and referrer headers, never put secrets there (chapter 6 of The Engineer's Citadel returns to this). And the term URI you'll see in specs is the broader category; for practical purposes a URL is a URI that tells you how to locate the thing, which is the only kind you'll use.

Origin: the web's security boundary

The three parts scheme, host and port together form the origin, and the origin is the single most important concept the web uses for security. The browser's same-origin policy keeps one site from reading another's data based on it; cookies, CORS and much else are defined in terms of it (all covered in the security stage). The example shows the rule's sharp edges: https and http on the same host are different origins, because the scheme differs, and app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins, because the host differs, even though they're the same site to a human. Getting "same origin" right is getting the scheme, host and port all equal.

Relative URLs and links

Most URLs in a page aren't written out in full; they're relative to the page's address, and the browser resolves them against a base. The example shows the rules: ./setup.html replaces the last path segment, ../api/ref.html climbs a directory, a leading / is absolute from the host's root, and a leading // is protocol-relative, keeping the current scheme but changing the host (handy for CDNs, and a classic open-redirect trap). Relative URLs are what make a site movable between domains without rewriting every link, and understanding resolution is what stops the mysterious "why did this link go there" bug.

Percent-encoding and schemes

A URL has structure, /, ?, &, # all mean something, so any data you put inside it that contains those characters must be percent-encoded (%26 for &, and so on), exactly as the example encodes "cats & dogs". This is the URL's version of the separate-data-from-structure rule you'll meet everywhere in security: encode data so it can't be mistaken for structure. Beyond http and https, the scheme can select other protocols entirely, ws and wss for WebSockets (chapter 7), mailto:, file:, data:, so the scheme is the first thing to check when a URL behaves unexpectedly.

Common traps
  • Putting secrets in the query string, where they leak into logs, history and referrers.
  • Assuming same host means same origin. Scheme and port count too; http and https differ.
  • Expecting the server to see the fragment. It never leaves the browser.
  • Building URLs by string concatenation, without percent-encoding the data you insert.
  • Missing protocol-relative // links, a common open-redirect and mixed-content source.
Exercises
Exercise 2.1Same origin?

The page is at https://shop.example.com/cart. For each, same origin or not, and why?

  1. https://shop.example.com/checkout
  2. https://shop.example.com:8443/cart
  3. http://shop.example.com/cart
  4. https://api.shop.example.com/cart
Show solution
  1. Same origin. Only the path differs, and the path isn't part of the origin.
  2. Different. The port differs (8443 vs the default 443).
  3. Different. The scheme differs (http vs https).
  4. Different. The host differs (api.shop vs shop), even though it's a subdomain of the same site. "Same site" and "same origin" are different ideas, which matters for cookies.
Exercise 2.2Resolve the links

A page at https://site.example/blog/2026/post.html contains these links. Where does each go?

  1. image.png
  2. /about
  3. ../2025/old.html
  4. //assets.site.example/style.css
Show solution
  1. https://site.example/blog/2026/image.png (same directory as the page).
  2. https://site.example/about (absolute path from the host root).
  3. https://site.example/blog/2025/old.html (up one directory, then down).
  4. https://assets.site.example/style.css (protocol-relative: keeps https, changes the host).

If you weren't sure, the chapter's urljoin example settles it, and it's exactly what the browser does.

Exercise 2.3Build the URL safely

You need to build a search URL for the user's query, which might contain spaces, ampersands or slashes. A colleague writes f"https://site.example/search?q={query}". What breaks, and what's the fix?

Show solution

If the query is a&b=c, the raw & and = are read as URL structure, so the server sees a parameter q=a and a bogus parameter b=c, not the intended search for "a&b=c". Spaces and slashes cause similar corruption or ambiguity. The fix is to percent-encode the value, which urlencode({"q": query}) does, turning it into q=a%26b%3Dc so it's carried as data, not structure. This is the same lesson as parameterised queries in a database: never build a structured string by concatenating untrusted data; use the encoder the format provides.

Checklist
  • Can you name every part of a URL and what it's for?
  • Do you know that an origin is scheme and host and port?
  • Do you understand that the fragment never reaches the server?
  • Do you percent-encode data you put into a URL?
  • Can you resolve a relative URL against a base in your head?
