Chapter 03

HTTP: the message

8 min read3 exercises

HTTP is a request-and-response protocol made of text: a line, some headers, a blank line, and an optional body. Learn its methods, its status codes, and above all how it marks where a message ends, because message framing is what your own server has to get right and where the subtle bugs live.

Text on the wire

An HTTP/1.1 request is simple enough to read and write by hand, which is exactly what this stage's deliverable asks you to do. It's a request line (method, target, version), a set of headers, a blank line, and an optional body. The response has the same shape with a status line instead. Parsing and building it is a few lines:

That small file is most of an HTTP server. The rest of this chapter is what the fields mean and the one thing the parser must never get wrong: framing.

Methods: what you want done

The method states the intent. The ones that matter, and two properties that govern them:

MethodMeansSafe?Idempotent?
GETFetch a resource; no side effectsyesyes
HEADLike GET but headers only, no bodyyesyes
POSTCreate, or submit; may have side effectsnono
PUTReplace a resource at a known URLnoyes
PATCHPartially updatenono
DELETERemove a resourcenoyes

Safe means it only reads, never changes state, so a crawler or a browser prefetch can call it freely (which is why putting a delete behind a GET is a classic bug). Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as once, which is what lets a client safely retry a timed-out PUT or DELETE but not a POST. These properties aren't enforced by HTTP; they're promises you keep when you implement the method, and the whole web (caches, retries, prefetching) assumes you keep them. The Engineer's Shipyard builds API design on top of this.

Status codes: how it went

The three-digit code's first digit is the category, and knowing the ranges is most of the job: 1xx informational (rare), 2xx success, 3xx redirection ("look elsewhere"), 4xx you (the client) got it wrong, 5xx I (the server) got it wrong. The ones worth memorising: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content; 301/308 permanent and 302/307 temporary redirects, 304 Not Modified (your cached copy is still good, chapter 4); 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 too many requests; 500 internal error, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout. The 4xx-versus-5xx line is the one that matters operationally: a spike in 4xx is usually a client or a bad deploy; a spike in 5xx is you.

Framing: where does the message end?

This is the question HTTP exists to answer on a byte stream, and the one your server must get exactly right. TCP gives you a stream of bytes with no message boundaries (chapter 9), so HTTP has to say where each message's body stops. There are two ways. Content-Length states the body's size up front, and the receiver reads exactly that many bytes, what build_response does. But sometimes you don't know the size when you start sending (a response generated on the fly), so chunked transfer-encoding sends the body as a series of sized chunks, each prefixed with its length in hex, ending with a zero-length chunk, which decode_chunked reassembles. Every HTTP/1.1 body uses one or the other. Getting framing wrong isn't just a bug; when a proxy and a server disagree about where a message ends, you get request smuggling, one of the nastier web vulnerabilities (The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 6), which is why the parser's handling of Content-Length and chunked has to be strict.

Keep-alive: reuse the connection

Opening a TCP connection costs a round trip (chapter 9), and HTTPS adds another for TLS (chapter 6), so opening a fresh connection for every request, as HTTP/1.0 did, is slow. HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default: after a response, the connection stays open (Connection: keep-alive) and the next request reuses it, paying the handshake once.

One subtlety the diagram flags: even with keep-alive, HTTP/1.1 sends requests serially on a connection, the next can't start until the previous response finishes (an attempt to overlap them, called pipelining, failed in practice because of head-of-line blocking). Browsers worked around it by opening six connections per host; HTTP/2 (chapter 5) solves it properly.

One more essential header: Host

HTTP/1.1 made the Host header mandatory, and it's why the modern web works: one server at one IP address can host thousands of sites, and the Host header tells it which one you want (virtual hosting). Without it, the IP address alone couldn't distinguish a.example from b.example on the same machine. It's also the header to be careful with on the server side, since trusting it blindly causes the cache-poisoning and password-reset bugs from The Engineer's Citadel.

Common traps
  • Side effects behind GET, which crawlers, prefetchers and caches will trigger.
  • Retrying a POST as if it were idempotent, causing duplicate charges or records.
  • Getting framing wrong: trusting both Content-Length and chunked, or miscounting bytes, the door to request smuggling.
  • Returning 200 with an error in the body, so clients, caches and monitoring can't tell success from failure.
  • Opening a new connection per request, paying the handshake every time.
Exercises
Exercise 3.1Choose the method and status

For each, give the HTTP method and the success status code.

  1. Create a new order and return it.
  2. Fetch an order.
  3. Replace an order's shipping address at a known URL.
  4. Delete an order, returning nothing.
Show solution
  1. POST /orders → 201 Created, with a Location header pointing to the new order.
  2. GET /orders/42 → 200 OK.
  3. PUT /orders/42/address → 200 OK (or 204). PUT because you're replacing at a known URL, and it's idempotent, so a retry is safe.
  4. DELETE /orders/42 → 204 No Content. Idempotent: deleting an already-deleted order can still return 204 (or 404).
Exercise 3.2Frame the response

Your socket server streams a large report it generates row by row, so it doesn't know the total size when the response starts. How do you frame the body, and what does the client see on the wire?

Show solution

Use chunked transfer-encoding: send Transfer-Encoding: chunked instead of Content-Length, then emit each batch of rows as a chunk, the size in hex, a CRLF, the bytes, a CRLF, and finish with a 0-size chunk and a final CRLF. The client reads chunks until the zero-size one, reassembling the body exactly as the chapter's decode_chunked does. This lets you start sending before you've finished generating, which is the whole point, and it's one of the two framing methods your deliverable must implement. Don't send both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding; a receiver that honours one while a proxy honours the other is the request-smuggling hole.

Exercise 3.3Diagnose the status codes

Your dashboard shows these shifts after a deploy. What does each most likely mean?

  1. A sudden wave of 500s.
  2. A wave of 404s on URLs that worked yesterday.
  3. A rise in 429s.
  4. Lots of 502s and 504s.
Show solution
  1. 500s: your code is throwing, a bug in the new deploy. Roll back and check logs.
  2. 404s on formerly-good URLs: a routing or deploy problem, a renamed path, a broken rewrite, a bad static-asset build, not the users' fault.
  3. 429s: clients are being rate-limited, maybe a retry storm, a misbehaving client, or limits set too low.
  4. 502/504: the gateway (a load balancer or proxy) can't reach or isn't getting timely answers from your backend, the backend is down, overloaded, or slow. The distinction from 500 tells you the failure is between the proxy and the server, not in the app's own logic.
Checklist
  • Can you read and write a raw HTTP/1.1 request and response?
  • Do you know which methods are safe and which are idempotent, and keep those promises?
  • Do you use status codes correctly, especially the 4xx-versus-5xx line?
  • Does your server frame bodies correctly, by Content-Length or chunked, never ambiguously?
  • Do you reuse connections with keep-alive rather than reconnecting per request?

Chapter 04

HTTP: caching, cookies and negotiation

7 min read3 exercises

HTTP is stateless by design: every request stands alone, which is what lets the web scale. On that foundation it adds three things that make it practical, caching so you don't fetch what you already have, cookies so a stateless protocol can remember you, and negotiation so one URL can serve the right format to each client.

Stateless by design

HTTP keeps no memory between requests: the server handles each one with no idea what you asked a moment ago. That sounds like a limitation, and it's actually the web's superpower, because any server can handle any request, so you can put a thousand servers behind a load balancer and it just works (chapter 18). The cost is that anything that should persist, who you are, what's in your cache, has to be carried explicitly, which is what this chapter's three mechanisms do.

Caching: the biggest lever there is

The fastest request is the one you never send. HTTP caching lets a response be reused, by the browser, a CDN, or a proxy in between, instead of fetched again, and getting it right is the single biggest performance win on the web. Two ideas drive it. Freshness: a response can carry Cache-Control: max-age=600, meaning "reuse me for 600 seconds without asking". Validation: when a cached copy goes stale, the cache doesn't blindly refetch; it asks "is my copy still good?" with the ETag it was given, and the server answers 304 Not Modified (keep it, a tiny response with no body) or sends a fresh 200. Here is the whole decision:

The trace shows it: a miss fetches and stores; within max-age it's a pure hit with no network; once stale it revalidates with the ETag and gets a 304, so it keeps the bytes it already had and just refreshes the freshness clock; and when the resource actually changes, revalidation returns 200 with the new body. That 304 is the quiet workhorse of the web: it turns "re-download the image" into "a few bytes confirming the image is unchanged".

A few more knobs matter in practice. no-store forbids caching entirely (for private, per-user data); no-cache confusingly means "cache it but always revalidate before use"; private lets the browser cache but not a shared CDN; s-maxage sets a separate lifetime for shared caches. And the Vary header tells caches which request headers change the response (Vary: Accept-Encoding), so they don't hand a gzipped copy to a client that can't decompress it. The pattern that makes static assets both cacheable forever and instantly updatable is to put a content hash in the filename (app.9f3c.js) and serve it with a one-year max-age: the URL changes when the content does.

Cookies: memory for a stateless protocol

To recognise you across requests, the server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc123 with a response, the browser stores it, and sends Cookie: session=abc123 on every subsequent request to that site. That round trip is how a stateless protocol gets state: the cookie is a little token the client carries back each time, and the server looks up who it belongs to. Cookies carry attributes that control their safety and scope, Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (hidden from JavaScript), SameSite (not sent on cross-site requests), Domain and Path (scope), and an expiry. The security of these is a whole topic in its own right (The Engineer's Citadel, chapter 5); here the point is the mechanism: state on the web is something the client carries, not something the connection remembers.

Content negotiation: one URL, many representations

The same resource can come in different forms, and the client says which it prefers through Accept headers, while the server picks and announces its choice with Content-Type. The main axes: type (Accept: application/json vs text/html), language (Accept-Language: fr), and encoding (Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd). That last one is quietly one of the web's biggest wins: the client advertises which compression it understands, the server compresses the response, and text payloads shrink by 70% or more over the wire, decompressed transparently by the browser. Whenever the response depends on one of these headers, the server must set Vary so caches key on it, the classic bug being a cache that serves a French page to an English visitor because it ignored Vary: Accept-Language.

Common traps
  • Caching per-user data in a shared cache, leaking one user's response to another, forgetting private or no-store.
  • No cache headers at all, so everything is refetched, or browsers guess.
  • Caching by URL while ignoring Vary, serving the wrong language or a gzipped body to a client that can't read it.
  • Confusing no-cache (revalidate) with no-store (never cache).
  • Not compressing text responses, leaving an easy 70% off the wire unclaimed.
Exercises
Exercise 4.1Set the cache headers

Choose Cache-Control (and any other cache headers) for each.

  1. A hashed static asset, app.9f3c.js.
  2. A logged-in user's account page.
  3. The home page, which changes a few times a day and is the same for everyone.
  4. A bank balance API response.
Show solution
  1. Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The content hash is in the URL, so it can be cached forever; a new build gets a new URL.
  2. Cache-Control: private, no-cache (plus an ETag). The browser may cache it, but a shared CDN must not, and it should revalidate before each use so a logout or change is seen.
  3. Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 with an ETag, perhaps s-maxage longer for the CDN with purging on publish. Short freshness plus cheap revalidation.
  4. Cache-Control: no-store. Sensitive, must never be written to any cache.
Exercise 4.2Trace the revalidation

Using the chapter's cache with max-age=10, a client requests the same image at t=0, t=8, and t=15, and the image hasn't changed. What happens at each, and how many bytes of body cross the network in total (body is 100 KB, a 304 is ~200 bytes)?

Show solution

t=0: miss, fetch 100 KB, store. t=8: still within max-age (8 < 10), a pure hit, no network. t=15: stale, so revalidate with the ETag; the image is unchanged, so the server returns 304, ~200 bytes, and the cache keeps its copy and refreshes freshness. Total body over the network: 100 KB once, plus a ~200-byte 304. Without validation you'd have refetched the full 100 KB at t=15; the ETag turned that into 200 bytes. Multiply by every image on every page view and the saving is the web's performance, much of it invisible, running on 304s.

Exercise 4.3Find the caching bug

Users report occasionally seeing another user's name on their dashboard, but only when behind a corporate proxy. The dashboard is served with Cache-Control: max-age=60. What's wrong?

Show solution

The response is per-user but marked max-age=60 with no private, so the shared corporate proxy cache is allowed to store one user's personalised dashboard and serve it to the next user who requests the same URL within 60 seconds. That's why it only happens behind the shared proxy and not for home users (whose browser cache is private to them). The fix is Cache-Control: private, no-store (or at least private) on anything personalised, so no shared cache ever holds it. This is a real and serious class of bug, a caching misconfiguration that becomes an information-disclosure vulnerability, which is why cache directives on authenticated responses deserve care.

Checklist
  • Does every response carry deliberate cache headers, not whatever the framework defaults to?
  • Is per-user data marked private or no-store so shared caches can't hold it?
  • Do you use ETags so stale content revalidates cheaply with 304s?
  • Do you set Vary whenever the response depends on a request header?
  • Are text responses compressed, and do you understand cookies as client-carried state?

Chapter 05

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

7 min read3 exercises

The HTTP you write (chapters 3 and 4) is the same across versions; what changed underneath is how messages share a connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection and HTTP/3 moves that onto QUIC to remove the last head-of-line blocking. Knowing the difference tells you why a page is fast, and why a lossy link makes one version crawl.

The problem each version solves

HTTP/1.1 sends requests one at a time per connection (chapter 3), so a page needing fifty resources is slow. Browsers worked around it by opening about six connections per host, but that's a hack: it's limited, and each connection pays its own handshake. The real fix is to carry many requests on one connection at once, which is multiplexing, and the story of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 is multiplexing done progressively better.

HTTP/2: many streams, one TCP connection

HTTP/2 keeps HTTP's meaning identical but changes the wire format from text to binary frames, and lets many streams share a single TCP connection, each stream an independent request/response, interleaved frame by frame. One connection now carries all fifty resources concurrently. It adds header compression (HPACK), because repetitive headers (cookies, user-agent) on every request waste bandwidth, and stream prioritisation. The result is a big speed-up over 1.1 for typical pages, and it's why HTTP/2 reached about 80% of top sites.

But HTTP/2 has a flaw it inherited from TCP. All those streams ride one TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes strictly in order: if one packet is lost, TCP holds back everything that arrived after it until the missing packet is retransmitted, a round trip later. So a single lost packet stalls every stream on the connection, even streams whose own data arrived fine. This is transport-level head-of-line blocking, and on a lossy link (mobile, congested Wi-Fi) it can make HTTP/2 slower than HTTP/1.1's six separate connections, because with six connections a loss only stalls one of them.

HTTP/3: multiplexing on QUIC

HTTP/3 fixes this by abandoning TCP. It runs over QUIC (RFC 9000), a transport built on UDP that provides its own streams, and crucially QUIC's streams are independent: a lost packet blocks only the stream whose data it carried, while every other stream keeps flowing. The head-of-line blocking is gone. QUIC brings three more wins because it was designed from scratch: the transport and TLS handshakes are combined into one round trip (and 0 round trips on resumption), so a fresh HTTPS connection is faster; it supports connection migration, so your download survives switching from Wi-Fi to cellular without starting over; and encryption is built in, not bolted on. The cost is that it's UDP, which some networks throttle or block, so clients fall back to HTTP/2 when QUIC can't get through.

The model shows the whole arc. With no loss, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 both crush HTTP/1.1 (one round versus four) by multiplexing. Under a single packet loss, HTTP/2's shared TCP pipe stalls all twenty streams while HTTP/3 delays only the one stream that lost a packet. That difference is the entire reason HTTP/3 exists.

What this means for you

Mostly, you turn it on. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are enabled at the server, load balancer or CDN, and because the semantics are unchanged, your application code and the headers of chapters 3 and 4 work as before. Two practical consequences, though. Old HTTP/1.1 performance hacks become counter-productive on HTTP/2: concatenating many files into one, "domain sharding" across hostnames, and inlining assets all fight multiplexing, so drop them. And protocol features are attack surface: in 2023 the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset attack (CVE-2023-44487) abused the cheapness of opening and instantly cancelling a stream to generate record-breaking denial-of-service floods, up to 398 million requests a second, a reminder that every new capability is also a new way to be attacked.

Common traps
  • Keeping HTTP/1.1 hacks (file concatenation, domain sharding, inlining) on HTTP/2, where they hurt.
  • Assuming HTTP/2 is always faster. On a lossy link its TCP head-of-line blocking can lose to 1.1.
  • Forgetting HTTP/3 needs UDP, which some networks block, so a fallback path must exist.
  • Thinking a new version changes HTTP's meaning. Methods, status codes and headers are the same.
  • Ignoring that multiplexing concentrates risk onto one connection and one protocol's quirks.
Exercises
Exercise 5.1Explain the mobile mystery

A page loads fast on your office Wi-Fi over HTTP/2 but is noticeably slower on a train, even when the connection has decent bandwidth. The site doesn't support HTTP/3. What's happening, and what would help?

Show solution

A train's mobile connection has packet loss, not just lower bandwidth, and HTTP/2 puts every stream on one TCP connection. Each lost packet triggers TCP head-of-line blocking: all your concurrent streams stall for a retransmission round trip, so the page stutters even though raw bandwidth is fine. What helps: HTTP/3, whose independent QUIC streams contain the loss to the one affected stream, which is exactly why it was designed and why it shines on mobile. (Ironically, old-style six-connection HTTP/1.1 would also localise the loss better than HTTP/2 here, which is the trap in exercise-style thinking that "newer is always faster".)

Exercise 5.2Audit the old optimisations

A site migrating to HTTP/2 still does these HTTP/1.1-era tricks. For each, keep or drop?

  1. Bundling 30 small JavaScript modules into one big file.
  2. Serving images from img1.site, img2.site, img3.site (domain sharding).
  3. Inlining a small critical CSS file into the HTML.
  4. Using a CDN.
Show solution
  1. Mostly drop. HTTP/2 multiplexes, so many small files are cheap to request, and separate files cache and update independently (a change to one module doesn't bust the whole bundle). Some bundling still helps compression and reduces per-file overhead, so it's a balance, not a hard rule.
  2. Drop. Sharding across hostnames forces multiple connections and defeats multiplexing (and each new host needs its own DNS lookup, connection and handshake). One connection is the goal now.
  3. Usually drop for large or shared CSS (it can't be cached separately), though inlining a tiny amount of truly critical CSS to avoid a round trip on first paint can still be worth it. Measure (chapter 16 of the AI volume's cousin, web perf).
  4. Keep. A CDN is orthogonal and even more valuable, and it's usually where you enable HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 in the first place (chapter 17).
Exercise 5.3Reason about QUIC's extras

Beyond fixing head-of-line blocking, name two things QUIC does that TCP+TLS can't, and why each matters.

Show solution
  • Combined handshake: QUIC merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into one round trip (zero on resumption), where TCP+TLS needs the TCP handshake then the TLS handshake, two round trips before any data. On a high-latency link that's a visible saving on every new connection.
  • Connection migration: a QUIC connection is identified by a connection ID, not the IP-address-and-port four-tuple, so it survives a network change, walking out of Wi-Fi onto cellular, without dropping and re-establishing. A TCP connection is bound to the four-tuple and breaks when your IP changes, forcing a reconnect. This matters enormously for mobile.

Both come from QUIC living in user space over UDP, free of TCP's decades of ossified assumptions, which is the deeper reason a new transport was worth the effort.

Checklist
  • Can you explain multiplexing and why it beats HTTP/1.1's serial connections?
  • Do you understand TCP head-of-line blocking, and why HTTP/2 suffers it but HTTP/3 doesn't?
  • Do you know HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP, with a combined handshake and connection migration?
  • Have you removed HTTP/1.1-era hacks that fight multiplexing?
  • Is there a fallback to HTTP/2 when QUIC is blocked?

Part II

Secure and real-time

Three chapters on what sits beside plain request-and-response: the TLS layer that makes it private and trustworthy, the transports that keep a connection open for real-time data, and the structured calls of RPC.

Chapter 06

TLS and HTTPS

7 min read3 exercises

HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS, which gives three things at once: no one can read the traffic, no one can tamper with it undetected, and you know you're really talking to the site you asked for. The first two come from encryption; the third, the hard one, comes from certificates and a chain of trust that ends at a root your device already trusts.

What TLS provides

TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL) sits between TCP and HTTP and turns a plain, readable connection into a secure one. It provides confidentiality, the bytes are encrypted, so a router, a Wi-Fi snooper or your ISP sees only ciphertext; integrity, any tampering is detected and the connection fails rather than delivering altered data; and authentication, you can be sure the server is who it claims to be. The first two are "just" encryption. The third is the part that makes the web trustworthy and the part most worth understanding, because encrypting a conversation with an impostor buys you nothing.

The handshake

Before any HTTP flows, client and server run a handshake to agree on keys and verify identity. TLS 1.3, the current version, does it in a single round trip:

Two things are happening at once. A key exchange (Diffie-Hellman) lets both sides derive the same secret key without ever sending it, using fresh, ephemeral keys per connection so that stealing the server's long-term key later can't decrypt past traffic (forward secrecy). And authentication: the server sends its certificate chain and signs the handshake, proving it holds the private key for the certificate. Connecting to a real server shows the result:

Certificates and the chain of trust

A certificate binds a public key to a name (example.com), and is signed by a certificate authority (CA). You don't trust the certificate because it says so; you trust it because you can follow its signatures up a chain to a root CA your device already trusts. Your operating system and browser ship with a list of a few hundred trusted root CAs, and validation means: the name matches the site, the dates are current, each certificate was really signed by the next one up, and the top is a trusted root. A real chain looks like this:

And the validation logic, which every browser runs on every connection, is only this:

The checks are exactly the ones an attacker must defeat, and the example shows each failing safely: a certificate for the wrong name, an expired one, one whose signature doesn't come from its stated issuer, and a chain that ends at a root nobody trusts. This is the whole security of HTTPS: anyone can generate a certificate claiming to be your bank, but they can't make it chain to a trusted root without a CA signing it. The weakness, that any of the hundreds of CAs can vouch for any name, is real, and the defences against a misbehaving CA (Certificate Transparency, pinning, shrinking lifetimes) are the subject of the security stage.

SNI, and serving many sites

One server at one IP address can host thousands of HTTPS sites, just as with the Host header (chapter 3), but there's a chicken-and-egg problem: the server must present the right certificate before the encrypted connection exists, so it can't read a Host header yet. The solution is Server Name Indication (SNI): the client puts the hostname in the ClientHello, in the clear, so the server knows which certificate to send. That cleartext hostname is the one piece of a TLS connection an eavesdropper can still see, which is why Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), standardised in 2026, now encrypts the SNI too, closing the last metadata leak.

Mutual TLS, and HTTPS everywhere

Normally only the server proves its identity. With mutual TLS (mTLS) the client presents a certificate as well, so both sides are authenticated, which is how services inside a system authenticate to each other without passwords (the zero-trust model of the production and security stages). And the web has moved to HTTPS by default: browsers mark plain HTTP as insecure, HSTS lets a site insist browsers only ever connect over HTTPS, and certificates are now free (via Let's Encrypt) and short-lived, which means the one rule you must follow is to automate renewal with ACME, because a manually-renewed certificate is an outage waiting for a date.

Common traps
  • Thinking encryption alone makes you safe. Without certificate validation you may have a private channel to an impostor.
  • Disabling certificate verification "to make it work", in a client or a test that reaches production.
  • Manually renewed certificates, which expire and take the site down.
  • Forgetting the extra round trip: a fresh HTTPS connection costs TCP + TLS handshakes before any data.
  • Assuming TLS hides everything. The SNI (without ECH) and the destination IP are still visible.
Exercises
Exercise 6.1Name the guarantee

Which TLS guarantee, confidentiality, integrity, or authentication, does each scenario rely on?

  1. Your password isn't readable by the coffee-shop Wi-Fi you're on.
  2. An ISP can't silently inject ads into a page you load.
  3. You're sure the login page is really your bank's, not a look-alike on the same network.
Show solution
  1. Confidentiality. Encryption means the Wi-Fi sees ciphertext.
  2. Integrity. TLS detects modification, so injected content breaks the connection rather than reaching you, this is why ISP ad-injection died with HTTPS.
  3. Authentication. The certificate chain proves the server holds a certificate for your bank's name, signed by a trusted CA; a look-alike can't produce one. Encryption without this (a) and (b) would still let you have a perfectly private conversation with the attacker.
Exercise 6.2Why did validation fail?

Using the chapter's verify_chain, a connection to shop.example fails. For each symptom, which check caught it?

  1. The certificate is for *.shop.example but presented for shop.example's API at api.other.example.
  2. The site's certificate expired yesterday.
  3. The browser says "issued by an unknown authority".
Show solution
  1. The name match check: the certificate's subject doesn't cover api.other.example. (Wildcards match one label, so even *.shop.example wouldn't cover a different domain.)
  2. The validity window check: now is past not_after. This is the "forgot to renew" outage, now mitigated by automation.
  3. The trusted root check: the chain ends at a root not in the device's trust store, a self-signed or private CA, or a chain the server failed to send completely. Browsers can't follow it to something they trust.
Exercise 6.3Count the round trips

A user on a connection with 80ms RTT loads https://new-site.example for the first time (not cached, not previously connected). Count the round trips before the first byte of HTML arrives, and where each goes.

Show solution
  • DNS (chapter 15): ~1 round trip to resolve the hostname to an IP (often local-cache fast, but cold here).
  • TCP handshake (chapter 9): 1 round trip (SYN, SYN-ACK, then the client can send).
  • TLS 1.3 handshake: 1 round trip.
  • HTTP request/response: 1 round trip for the client's GET and the server's first bytes.

That's roughly 4 round trips ≈ 320ms of pure network latency before any HTML, no matter how fast the server or your code. It's why connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2), TLS resumption, QUIC's 0-RTT, and a nearby CDN (chapter 17) matter so much: they remove round trips, and round trips are the thing you can't speed up by optimising code.

Checklist
  • Can you name TLS's three guarantees, and why authentication is the hard one?
  • Do you understand the handshake derives a shared key without sending it, with forward secrecy?
  • Can you explain certificate validation: name, dates, signature chain, trusted root?
  • Do you know what SNI is and why it (without ECH) leaks the hostname?
  • Are your certificates renewed automatically?

Chapter 07

Real-time transports

6 min read3 exercises

Plain HTTP is one-shot and client-initiated: you ask, the server answers, done. Real-time features, chat, live scores, collaborative editing, need the server to push, or two sides to talk continuously. There's a ladder of techniques, from faking it with repeated polling up to true bidirectional connections, and the skill is picking the simplest rung that meets the need.

The problem: HTTP only answers when asked

In the request/response model, the server can't speak until the client asks, so "notify me the moment something happens" doesn't fit. Four approaches bridge the gap, each keeping a connection open longer than the last:

The ladder, rung by rung

  • Short polling. The client just asks again every few seconds. Trivial to build, works over any HTTP, but wasteful (most replies are "nothing new") and laggy (updates wait for the next poll). Fine for data that changes slowly and tolerates delay.
  • Long polling. The client asks, and the server holds the response open until there's something to send, then answers and the client immediately asks again. Near-real-time with ordinary HTTP, which is why it was the web's workhorse for years, but it's still one message per request and ties up a connection.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE). The client opens one long-lived HTTP response and the server streams events down it as they happen, a simple text format, one per block. It's built into browsers (EventSource), reconnects automatically, and runs over plain HTTP, but it's one-way (server to client) and text-only. Ideal for feeds, notifications, live dashboards, progress, and token streaming from an AI model.
  • WebSocket. A single, persistent, full-duplex connection: after an upgrade handshake, either side can send a message at any time, as binary or text, with low overhead. The right tool for chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing, anything genuinely two-way.

The WebSocket upgrade

A WebSocket is clever about starting: it begins as an ordinary HTTP request that asks to upgrade the connection, so it works through the same ports, proxies and firewalls as HTTPS. The server proves it understood by hashing the client's key with a fixed magic string and returning 101 Switching Protocols; after that, the TCP connection is a WebSocket and no longer speaks HTTP.

The accept-key computation matches the RFC's own test vector exactly, which is how a server (and the browser) confirm the peer really speaks WebSocket and that no cache or proxy mangled the handshake. The magic string serves no cryptographic purpose; it just makes an accidental upgrade impossible.

WebRTC and WebTransport

Two more sit at the specialised ends. WebRTC is built for peer-to-peer real-time media, video calls, voice, between browsers directly, which means solving hard problems TLS and TCP don't: punching through NATs (chapter 14) with STUN and TURN servers, and tolerating loss over UDP because a dropped video frame should be skipped, not retransmitted (chapter 11). It also offers data channels. It's the right, if heavy, tool for conferencing. WebTransport is the newest arrival, reaching cross-browser support in 2026: it runs over HTTP/3 and QUIC, giving multiplexed streams and unreliable datagrams over one connection with no head-of-line blocking (chapter 5), effectively a modern WebSocket that also does the lossy-datagram job WebRTC data channels did. For new client-server real-time work on HTTP/3, it's increasingly the answer; WebSocket remains the safe, universal default.

Common traps
  • Reaching for WebSockets when SSE would do. One-way updates don't need a bidirectional connection.
  • Short polling a fast-changing resource, hammering the server for mostly-empty answers.
  • Forgetting WebSockets aren't HTTP after the upgrade, so HTTP caching, status codes and many proxies don't apply.
  • Using WebRTC for simple server push, paying for NAT traversal and media machinery you don't need.
  • No reconnect/backoff logic: long-lived connections drop, and the client must re-establish gracefully.
Exercises
Exercise 7.1Pick the transport

Choose a real-time approach for each, and justify it.

  1. Streaming an AI model's answer token by token to the browser.
  2. A two-player chess game.
  3. A stock ticker updating a few prices every second, display only.
  4. A group video call.
Show solution
  1. Server-Sent Events. It's one-way (server to client), text, and streaming, exactly SSE's shape, with automatic reconnection for free. No need for a bidirectional WebSocket.
  2. WebSocket (or WebTransport on HTTP/3). Moves are bidirectional and need low latency; both players send at any time.
  3. SSE, again one-way streaming. Short polling would also work but wastes requests; SSE pushes only when a price changes.
  4. WebRTC, which is built for peer-to-peer media with NAT traversal and loss tolerance. The others aren't designed for real-time audio/video.
Exercise 7.2Reason about the handshake

Why does a WebSocket start as an HTTP request instead of just opening a new kind of connection on a new port? And what does the Sec-WebSocket-Accept hash protect against?

Show solution

Starting as HTTP(S) means WebSockets ride the same ports (80/443), TLS, proxies, firewalls and load balancers as normal web traffic, so they work from locked-down networks where a new port would be blocked, and they can share infrastructure with the rest of the site. The Sec-WebSocket-Accept hash (SHA-1 of the client's key plus the magic GUID) proves the server actually understood the WebSocket upgrade and isn't, say, a caching proxy or an old server blindly echoing a 101; it prevents a non-WebSocket endpoint from accidentally being treated as one, and stops certain cache-poisoning tricks. It's a handshake-confirmation, not encryption, security comes from running over wss:// (TLS).

Exercise 7.3Design for the drop

Your WebSocket-based collaborative editor works in the office but users on mobile report losing changes when they go through a tunnel or switch networks. What's happening, and how do you make it robust?

Show solution

Long-lived connections drop, when the network blips, a NAT or load balancer times out an idle connection, or the device changes IP (Wi-Fi to cellular), which breaks the TCP connection the WebSocket rides on (chapter 5, 9). Robustness means treating disconnection as normal: detect it (heartbeat/ping frames with a timeout), reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and, crucially, make the application recover state, buffer unsent changes locally and replay them, and on reconnect resynchronise from a server sequence number so nothing is lost or duplicated. For the network-switch case specifically, WebTransport over QUIC (with connection migration, chapter 5) survives the IP change that kills a WebSocket. The deeper lesson: a persistent connection is a convenience, not a guarantee; design as if it will drop, because it will.

Checklist
  • Do you pick the simplest rung, SSE for one-way, WebSocket for two-way, that meets the need?
  • Do you understand SSE is one-way over plain HTTP, WebSocket is full-duplex after an upgrade?
  • Do you know WebRTC is for peer-to-peer media and WebTransport for HTTP/3-era client-server?
  • Does every long-lived connection have heartbeat, reconnect and backoff?
  • Does the application recover cleanly when a connection drops?

Chapter 08

RPC and schemas

8 min read3 exercises

A remote procedure call makes talking to another service look like calling a function. Underneath, the arguments are serialised, sent over the network, and decoded on the far side, and the contract that keeps both sides agreeing is a schema. The deep skill is schema evolution: changing that contract without breaking the services already running against it.

Calling a function on another machine

Much of a modern system is services calling other services, and RPC (remote procedure call) makes that look like an ordinary function call: you call getUser(42) and get a user back, while a framework handles turning the call into bytes, sending them, and turning the reply back into an object. The convenience is real and the danger is that it hides the network: a local call can't be slow for 200 milliseconds, fail halfway, or vanish, and a remote one can (the fallacies of distributed computing, which the distributed-systems stage covers). So treat RPC as a networked operation with timeouts, retries and error handling, not as a function that happens to live elsewhere.

gRPC and the alternatives

The dominant RPC framework, gRPC, runs over HTTP/2 (chapter 5), sends compact binary messages, and supports streaming in both directions, not just one request and one response but server streams, client streams and bidirectional streams. It generates strongly-typed client and server code from a schema, so a mismatch is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. That makes it excellent for service-to-service traffic inside a system, where speed and strict contracts matter and humans aren't reading the wire. Its trade-off against plain REST (HTTP plus JSON, chapters 3 and 4) is the usual one: REST is human-readable, browser-native and loosely coupled; gRPC is faster, typed and stricter but not directly usable from a browser (which can't control HTTP/2 frames), needing a gRPC-Web or Connect proxy. Rule of thumb: REST or JSON for public and browser-facing APIs, gRPC for internal service meshes where you control both ends.

Protocol Buffers: the wire format

gRPC serialises with Protocol Buffers (protobuf): you write a schema listing each field with a number, and the encoder puts those numbers, not the field names, on the wire, with the values packed tightly. This is both why protobuf is small and fast and why it evolves gracefully. Here is the whole encoding, small enough to hold in your head:

The message {id: 42, name: "widget"} is ten bytes, and the hex shows why: each field is a tag (the field number and a type) followed by the value, no field names anywhere. JSON would spell out "id" and "name" on every message; protobuf never does.

Schema evolution: the skill that matters

Services deploy independently, so at any moment an old sender may talk to a new receiver or the reverse, and the schema must change without breaking either. Because the wire identifies fields by number, the rules are precise, and the example demonstrates each:

  • Renaming a field is safe. The example decodes the same bytes with field 2 called name and then label, both work, because the wire only ever had the number 2. Names are for your code, not the wire.
  • Adding a field is safe, as long as it gets a new number. The old decoder, shown reading a message that includes a new field 3, keeps it as an unknown field and carries on, which is forward compatibility: new senders don't break old receivers.
  • Never change or reuse a field number. The last line reuses number 2, once a string, now an integer price_cents, and old data silently decodes into garbage: price_cents comes out as the bytes of "widget". No error, just corruption, which is far worse than a crash. When you remove a field, you mark its number reserved so it can never be reused.

These rules, never change or reuse a number, only add with new numbers, are the whole discipline of evolving a binary contract, and they're the same idea as additive, backward-compatible API changes in The Engineer's Shipyard. Get them wrong and you get the quietest, nastiest bug there is: two services that both "work" but disagree about what the bytes mean.

Beyond protobuf

Protobuf is one of a family of schema-based binary formats (Avro and Thrift are others), all solving the same problem: a compact, fast, evolvable encoding with a contract both sides share. The alternative, schemaless JSON, trades size and speed for human-readability and needing no shared schema, which is exactly the right trade for public APIs and anything a person debugs by eye. The choice isn't gRPC-versus-REST as tribes; it's binary-and-typed where you own both ends and want speed, text-and-flexible where you don't.

Common traps
  • Treating an RPC like a local call, with no timeout, retry or failure handling.
  • Reusing or renumbering protobuf fields, silently corrupting data across versions.
  • Making a breaking schema change and deploying both services at once, hoping nothing is in flight.
  • Reaching for gRPC in the browser, which can't speak it without a proxy.
  • Using binary protobuf for a public API that outside developers must read and debug.
Exercises
Exercise 8.1Classify the schema changes

For each change to a protobuf message, safe or breaking, and why?

  1. Rename field 5 from qty to quantity.
  2. Add field 9, a new optional notes string.
  3. Change field 3 from int32 to string.
  4. Delete field 4, then later add field 4 as a new discount.
Show solution
  1. Safe. The wire uses the number 5; the name is only in your code.
  2. Safe. A new number means old receivers ignore it and new ones read it, backward and forward compatible.
  3. Breaking. Same number, different type: old integers decode as garbage under the new type and vice versa. Add a new field with a new number instead.
  4. Breaking. Reusing number 4 means old messages carrying the old field 4 are misread as discount. When you delete a field, reserve its number forever so this can't happen.
Exercise 8.2REST or gRPC?

Choose for each, and say why.

  1. A public API third-party developers will integrate against.
  2. High-volume calls between your pricing service and your checkout service.
  3. A browser app talking directly to your backend.
  4. Streaming live telemetry from thousands of devices to a collector.
Show solution
  1. REST/JSON. Public, human-debuggable, browser- and tool-friendly, no schema to distribute, no proxy needed.
  2. gRPC. You own both ends; binary protobuf over HTTP/2 is faster and the typed contract catches mismatches at build time.
  3. REST/JSON, or gRPC-Web/Connect if you want the typed contract, since a browser can't speak raw gRPC.
  4. gRPC streaming, whose bidirectional streams and compact binary suit continuous, high-volume telemetry well.
Exercise 8.3Ship the schema change safely

You need to split a protobuf name field into first_name and last_name across two services deployed independently. Outline the safe sequence.

Show solution
  1. Add, don't replace: add first_name and last_name as new fields with new numbers, keeping the old name field.
  2. Deploy the senders to populate all three fields (old and new) during the transition, so every receiver, old or new, has what it needs.
  3. Deploy the receivers to read the new fields, falling back to parsing name if the new ones are empty (for messages still in flight from not-yet-updated senders).
  4. Once everything reads the new fields and no old data remains, stop writing name, and eventually remove it, reserve-ing its number.

At no point is there a flag day where both must change together; each step is backward compatible, which is the whole point of the field-number discipline, and the same expand-then-contract pattern used for database and API migrations elsewhere in the series.

Checklist
  • Do you treat every RPC as a network call, with timeouts and failure handling?
  • Do you understand that protobuf identifies fields by number, not name?
  • Do you only ever add fields with new numbers, and never change or reuse a number?
  • Do you reserve the numbers of removed fields?
  • Do you choose REST/JSON for public and browser APIs, gRPC for internal service traffic?

Part III

Transport

Four chapters down a layer, to how bytes actually get delivered. TCP's reliable connection and its fight against congestion, UDP's deliberate simplicity, and the socket API that every client and server in this book is built on.

Chapter 09

TCP: connection and reliability

7 min read3 exercises

IP delivers packets that may be lost, duplicated or reordered, and makes no promises. TCP builds on top of it the thing almost everything you write depends on: a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two programs. It does it with a handshake to start, sequence numbers to order, and acknowledgements and retransmission to recover loss.

A reliable stream over an unreliable network

The network layer (IP, chapter 13) is deliberately dumb: it forwards packets and that's all, so a packet can vanish in a full router queue, arrive twice, or overtake an earlier one. TCP's job is to hide all of that and present your program with a clean byte stream, what you write comes out the other end, in order, complete, or the connection fails honestly. It achieves this entirely at the two endpoints (the end-to-end principle, chapter 1), using three mechanisms: a handshake, sequence numbers, and acknowledgement with retransmission.

The three-way handshake

Before any data, the two sides synchronise with three messages: the client sends SYN (with its starting sequence number), the server replies SYN-ACK (acknowledging the client's and sending its own), and the client sends ACK. Now both know each other's sequence numbers and that the path works in both directions.

The handshake costs one round trip before a single byte of data, which is the floor on every new TCP connection's latency, and the reason HTTPS, adding TLS's handshake on top, costs two (chapter 6). A connection is identified by the four-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port), so one server can hold millions of connections at once, each distinguished by the client's address and port, and this is also what NAT (chapter 14) rewrites and what QUIC (chapter 5) escapes to survive network changes.

Sequence numbers and acknowledgement

Every byte in the stream has a sequence number, and the receiver sends back cumulative acknowledgements: "I have everything up to byte N, send me N next". If a segment is lost, later segments may still arrive, but the ACK stops advancing, pointing at the gap, and the receiver buffers the out-of-order data until the missing piece arrives. The sender keeps a copy of everything un-acknowledged and retransmits it, on a timeout, or faster when it sees repeated ACKs for the same byte (three duplicate ACKs trigger a fast retransmit). Here is that whole mechanism:

Watch the ACK in the trace. After the segment at byte 4 is lost, the next segment (byte 8) arrives, but the ACK stays at 4, because TCP acknowledges the stream only up to the first gap, that's the cumulative part. The receiver holds byte 8 in its buffer. When the sender retransmits byte 4, the ACK jumps all the way to 12, acknowledging both the retransmitted segment and the buffered one at once. The stream is delivered intact, in order, despite the loss, which is TCP's entire promise kept in a dozen lines.

Teardown, and the states

Closing is a four-message dance: each side sends a FIN and gets an ACK, because the stream is independently closable in each direction. After its final ACK, a side sits in TIME_WAIT for a while before fully releasing the connection, to make sure a late, duplicated packet from this connection can't be mistaken for a new one reusing the same four-tuple. A server with huge numbers of connections in TIME_WAIT is a real operational issue you'll meet, and it's a direct consequence of this safety rule. TCP tracks a connection through a set of states (LISTEN, SYN-SENT, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT, TIME_WAIT and the rest), which the diagnosis tools of chapter 19 let you watch.

Common traps
  • Forgetting the handshake's round trip, and opening a new connection per request when you could reuse one.
  • Assuming TCP preserves message boundaries. It's a byte stream; your two sends may arrive as one recv or split across several (chapter 12).
  • Expecting instant failure. A lost connection can take many seconds of retransmission timeouts to be declared dead.
  • Running out of ephemeral ports or piling up TIME_WAIT under high connection churn.
  • Thinking an ACK means the application processed the data. It means TCP received it; the app may not have read it yet.
Exercises
Exercise 9.1Read the cumulative ACK

Four 4-byte segments are sent: bytes 0, 4, 8, 12. Segment 4 is lost; 0, 8, 12 arrive. What ACK does the receiver send after each arrival, and why doesn't it jump ahead when 8 and 12 arrive?

Show solution

After byte-0 arrives: ACK 4 (have 0–3, want 4). After byte-8 arrives (4 still missing): ACK 4 again, the cumulative ACK can only report the stream up to the first gap, and there's a hole at 4, so it can't acknowledge 8 even though it has it (it buffers it). After byte-12: ACK 4 once more. These repeated ACKs for 4 are the duplicate ACKs that tell the sender "4 is missing, everything after it is waiting", and three of them trigger a fast retransmit. Once 4 is retransmitted and arrives, the ACK leaps to 16, acknowledging 4, 8 and 12 all at once from the buffer.

Exercise 9.2Count the round trips, again

A client with 100ms RTT makes a single small HTTPS request to a server it has never connected to (ignore DNS). Break down the round trips from the first packet to the response, and say which ones connection reuse removes.

Show solution
  • TCP handshake: 1 RTT (SYN, SYN-ACK; the client can send data with its ACK).
  • TLS 1.3 handshake: 1 RTT (chapter 6).
  • HTTP request/response: 1 RTT.

About 3 RTT = 300ms before the response, all network, none of it the server's code. Keep-alive and HTTP/2 remove the TCP and TLS handshakes on subsequent requests (reuse the connection), TLS session resumption removes a TLS round trip on reconnect, and QUIC/HTTP/3 folds transport and TLS into one (and zero on resumption). The whole performance game at this layer is removing round trips, because you cannot make a round trip faster than the speed of light allows (chapter 16).

Exercise 9.3Explain the slow failure

A service calls another over TCP. The callee's machine is yanked off the network (not a clean shutdown). The caller hangs for 30 seconds before erroring. Why so long, and what should the caller have done?

Show solution

Because nothing told the caller the peer was gone, there was no FIN, just silence. TCP can't distinguish "the network is slow" from "the peer vanished", so it retransmits the un-acknowledged data with exponentially increasing timeouts and only gives up after many attempts, which can be tens of seconds to minutes. This is the fallacy "the network is reliable" made concrete. The caller should not rely on TCP's own timeout: set an application-level timeout on the request (a few seconds), so it fails fast and can retry, fall back, or shed load, which is exactly the timeout discipline the distributed-systems and reliability stages insist on. A silent peer is the common case, not the exception.

Checklist
  • Can you describe the three-way handshake and why it costs a round trip?
  • Do you understand cumulative ACKs and how loss is detected and retransmitted?
  • Do you know a connection is identified by its four-tuple?
  • Do you remember TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries?
  • Do you set application-level timeouts rather than trusting TCP to fail fast?

Chapter 10

TCP: flow and congestion control

7 min read3 exercises

A sender has two ways to go too fast: overwhelm the receiver, or overwhelm the network. TCP guards against the first with flow control, a window the receiver advertises, and against the second with congestion control, a window the sender probes blindly, ramping up until loss and backing off. Together they decide how much of a link you actually get.

Two different "slow down" problems

TCP's reliability (chapter 9) is only half the story; the other half is how fast to send, and there are two independent limits. Flow control stops a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver: the receiver advertises, in every ACK, a receive window, how much buffer space it has free, and the sender never has more unacknowledged data in flight than that. It's a simple, explicit signal from the one place that knows. Congestion control is the hard one: it stops senders from overwhelming the network in between, which has no voice to say "stop". The sender must infer congestion, and traditionally the only signal it has is packet loss.

The sawtooth: probe, back off, repeat

Lacking a dial marked "network capacity", TCP discovers it by probing. It starts cautiously and ramps up fast (slow start: double the window each round trip), until it hits a threshold or loses a packet; then it grows gently (congestion avoidance: add one each round trip), nosing upward until loss appears again; and on loss it cuts the window sharply (multiplicative decrease: halve it). The result, additive increase and multiplicative decrease (AIMD), is the characteristic sawtooth:

The code produces exactly this shape: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 while doubling, then 17, 18 adding one, then a loss halves it to 9, it climbs again, another loss halves it to 7. The average of that sawtooth is the throughput you actually get, which is why a lossy link (chapter 5's mobile case) gives you so much less than its raw bandwidth: every loss knocks the window down.

The bandwidth-delay product

How much data must be "in flight" (sent but not yet acknowledged) to keep a link busy? Exactly the bandwidth-delay product: bandwidth multiplied by round-trip time. The example computes it: to fill a 100 Mbps link with an 80ms RTT, you need about 977 KB in flight at once. If your window is smaller, you stall waiting for ACKs and never reach the link's speed, the old 64 KB maximum window would cap that fast, far link at a miserable 7 Mbps. This is why high-bandwidth, high-latency paths ("long fat networks", a satellite link, a transcontinental fibre) need large windows, and why window scaling was added to TCP. The lesson generalises: on a fast but distant link, throughput is limited by your window and the RTT, not by the bandwidth you're paying for.

CUBIC, BBR, and bufferbloat

Classic loss-based congestion control has a flaw: to detect congestion it must cause loss, which means it keeps network buffers full, and a full buffer adds latency to everything behind it. That's bufferbloat: a big download makes a video call stutter not because bandwidth ran out but because the buffer filled with the download's packets and everything now waits in a long queue. The default algorithm on most systems, CUBIC, is loss-based and prone to this. Google's BBR takes a different approach: instead of waiting for loss, it models the path, measuring the bottleneck bandwidth and the minimum round-trip time, and sends just enough to fill the pipe without filling the buffers, so it keeps throughput high and latency low. As of 2026 CUBIC is still the common default, BBR is widely used by large services, and the fight against bufferbloat also runs in the routers themselves, through smarter queue management. You rarely choose the algorithm, but knowing why a download tanks your latency, and that it needn't, is the point.

Common traps
  • Expecting to get a link's full bandwidth over a high-latency path with a small window.
  • Blaming bandwidth for latency under load, when it's bufferbloat, a full queue, not a full pipe.
  • Treating any loss as a disaster. Loss is how loss-based TCP finds the limit; a little is normal.
  • Confusing flow control with congestion control. One protects the receiver, the other the network.
  • Opening many parallel connections to "go faster", grabbing more than a fair share and worsening congestion for everyone.
Exercises
Exercise 10.1Size the window

You're copying a large file between two data centres on opposite coasts: a 1 Gbps link with 70ms RTT. The transfer only reaches ~150 Mbps. Using the bandwidth-delay product, explain why, and what to change.

Show solution

To fill 1 Gbps at 70ms RTT you need BDP = 1,000,000,000 / 8 × 0.070 ≈ 8.75 MB in flight. If the TCP window (limited by the receiver's buffer or OS settings) is, say, ~1 MB, you can only have 1 MB outstanding per RTT, giving 1 MB / 0.070s ≈ 114 Mbps, roughly what you see. The fix is to raise the TCP buffer sizes so the window can grow to at least the BDP (window scaling must be on, which it is by default now, but the buffers cap it). This is the classic "long fat network" problem: on a fast, distant link, your window, not the bandwidth, is the bottleneck.

Exercise 10.2Diagnose the stutter

Whenever someone on the home Wi-Fi starts a big upload, everyone else's video calls stutter and web pages crawl, even though the connection "has plenty of bandwidth". What's happening, and what helps?

Show solution

Bufferbloat. The upload's loss-based congestion control fills the router's (often oversized) buffer to find the capacity, and now every other packet, the video call's, the web request's, sits behind a long queue of upload packets, adding hundreds of milliseconds of latency. It's not that bandwidth ran out; it's that the queue got deep. Fixes: enable modern active queue management (fq_codel/CAKE) on the router, which keeps queues short and shares them fairly; use a congestion-control algorithm like BBR that doesn't fill buffers; and set a sane upload rate limit if the router is dumb. The deep lesson: latency and bandwidth are different resources, and a fat pipe with a bloated buffer can be a slow one.

Exercise 10.3Read the sawtooth

In the chapter's simulation, why does the window grow exponentially at first but only linearly after the threshold? What would happen to a new connection that stays in slow start the whole time?

Show solution

Slow start grows exponentially (doubling) to find the available bandwidth fast, since a new connection has no idea how much it can use and starting at one segment per round trip would waste a fast link for ages. But exponential growth would blow straight past the capacity and cause heavy loss, so once TCP is near where it last saw congestion (the threshold), it switches to additive increase, nudging up by one per round trip to probe gently. A connection that stayed in slow start would keep doubling until it caused significant loss, overshooting badly, which is exactly why the threshold and the switch to avoidance exist. The two phases are "find the ballpark quickly" then "approach the edge carefully".

Checklist
  • Can you distinguish flow control (protects the receiver) from congestion control (protects the network)?
  • Do you understand slow start, congestion avoidance, and the AIMD sawtooth?
  • Can you compute the bandwidth-delay product and see why a small window throttles a fast, far link?
  • Do you know what bufferbloat is and why a big transfer can wreck latency?
  • Do you know loss-based (CUBIC) and model-based (BBR) control differ, and how?

Chapter 11

UDP, and when losing packets is right

7 min read3 exercises

UDP is almost nothing: it adds ports and a checksum to raw IP, and that's all, no handshake, no reliability, no ordering, no congestion control. That sounds worse than TCP until you meet the cases where TCP's guarantees are exactly wrong, where a packet that arrives late is useless, and dropping it is better than waiting for it.

The minimal transport

Where TCP is an elaborate machine for reliability and ordering (chapters 9 and 10), UDP is a thin shim over IP. It adds just two things: ports, so the packet reaches the right program, and an optional checksum to detect corruption. There's no connection to set up, no acknowledgements, no retransmission, no ordering, no flow or congestion control. You send a datagram and it either arrives or it doesn't, and you find out neither way. UDP is also message-oriented: each send is one datagram with preserved boundaries, unlike TCP's shapeless byte stream (chapter 9), which is often reason enough to pick it.

This looks like a downgrade, and for fetching a web page it is, which is why the web runs on TCP. But "the network guarantees nothing and neither do I" is precisely what some applications want, because it hands them control over the trade-offs TCP makes for everyone.

When losing a packet is the right call

TCP's cardinal rule, deliver every byte, in order, becomes a liability the moment data has a deadline. Consider a live voice call:

One audio frame is lost. TCP, insisting on in-order delivery, holds back not just the lost frame but every frame behind it until the retransmission arrives a round trip later, and in a live call that round trip is an eternity: six frames miss their moment to be played, a long audible gap. UDP simply skips the lost frame, the codec conceals the 20-millisecond hole, and the conversation stays in sync: one tiny glitch instead of a stutter. A late packet is a useless packet here, so retransmitting it is worse than forgetting it. That's the whole case for UDP.

Where UDP belongs

  • Real-time media (voice, video, live streaming): skip losses and conceal them; never stall the stream to recover old data. This is why WebRTC (chapter 7) uses UDP.
  • Live games: send the latest world state; a dropped older state is worthless, so don't retransmit it, send the new one.
  • DNS (chapter 15): one tiny request, one tiny reply; a connection handshake would cost more than the query, so DNS uses UDP and retries at the application layer if an answer doesn't come.
  • A foundation to build on: when you want some of TCP's guarantees but not all, or want control TCP can't give, you build your own transport over UDP. That's exactly what QUIC (chapter 5) is: reliability and ordering per stream, its own congestion control, and encryption, all on top of UDP, in user space, free of TCP's rigidity.

What you take on, and the dangers

Choosing UDP means choosing responsibility. Anything you need, reliability, ordering, rate limiting, you must add yourself or deliberately do without. Two dangers in particular. First, no congestion control means a naive UDP application can flood a network and contribute to congestion collapse, which is why every serious UDP protocol (including QUIC) implements congestion control of its own, and why you should never just blast datagrams as fast as you can. Second, amplification attacks: because UDP has no handshake, an attacker can spoof a victim's address as the source of a small request to a server that replies with a much larger response (DNS and NTP are classic amplifiers), turning the server into an unwitting weapon aimed at the victim. It's a reason UDP services must limit response sizes to unverified senders, and a reason the Mirai-era DDoS attacks hit so hard.

Common traps
  • Reaching for UDP for ordinary data transfer, then reinventing TCP, badly, on top of it.
  • Sending UDP as fast as you can, with no congestion control, hurting the network and yourself.
  • Assuming datagrams arrive, in order, intact. None of that is promised; design for loss and reorder.
  • Building an open UDP service that amplifies small requests into big replies, a DDoS tool.
  • Forgetting UDP datagrams have a size limit (and fragment badly above the path MTU).
Exercises
Exercise 11.1TCP or UDP?

Choose for each, and say why.

  1. Downloading a software update.
  2. A multiplayer shooter sending player positions 60 times a second.
  3. A single DNS lookup.
  4. Live-streaming a sports match with sub-second latency.
Show solution
  1. TCP. Every byte must arrive, in order; a corrupted update is useless, and there's no deadline that makes a retransmit too late. Reliability is exactly what you want.
  2. UDP. Positions are time-sensitive and self-superseding, a dropped old position is worthless because a newer one is already on the way. Retransmitting it would show the player in the past.
  3. UDP. One small request and reply; a TCP handshake would triple the cost. The resolver retries at the application layer if needed (and falls back to TCP for large answers).
  4. UDP-based (WebRTC or a QUIC-based transport): low latency matters more than perfect delivery, and a dropped frame is concealed rather than stalling the stream. A buffered, non-live stream, by contrast, can use TCP.
Exercise 11.2Reason about the deadline

In the chapter's model, why does one lost frame glitch six frames under TCP but only one under UDP? What would reduce the TCP number (short of switching to UDP)?

Show solution

Under TCP, the lost frame can't be delivered until its retransmission arrives ~1 RTT (120ms) later, and because TCP delivers in order, every frame that arrives in the meantime is held in the buffer behind the gap. With 20ms frames, 120ms of waiting means six frames (the lost one plus the five that arrive during the wait) all miss their playout deadlines, this is head-of-line blocking (chapter 5) applied to audio. UDP delivers each frame independently, so only the actually-lost one glitches. To reduce the TCP number without leaving TCP you'd need a bigger jitter/playout buffer (delay playback enough to cover a retransmit), but that adds constant latency to the whole call, which for a conversation is itself a problem. There's no free lunch: TCP trades latency for completeness, and real-time wants the opposite trade.

Exercise 11.3Build on UDP responsibly

You're writing a custom protocol over UDP for a game. List what you must add yourself, and one danger to avoid.

Show solution
  • Only the reliability you actually need: perhaps reliable, ordered delivery for chat and inventory changes, but unreliable, unordered for position updates (send the latest, drop the rest). Mixing both per message type is the point of building your own.
  • Congestion control, or at least rate limiting, so you don't flood the network, this is non-negotiable and the reason QUIC includes it.
  • Sequence numbers to detect loss and reordering where you care, and to discard stale data.
  • Message framing within the datagram limit, keeping messages under the path MTU to avoid fragmentation.
  • The danger: an unauthenticated, amplifying endpoint (small request, big reply) that attackers can abuse for DDoS, require a handshake or a token before sending large responses to a new address, as QUIC does. Honestly, unless you have a strong reason, building on QUIC rather than raw UDP gives you most of this correctly for free.
Checklist
  • Can you explain what UDP adds to IP, and what it deliberately leaves out?
  • Do you understand why a late packet is useless for real-time, so loss beats delay?
  • Do you know UDP is message-oriented, where TCP is a byte stream?
  • If you build on UDP, do you add congestion control and only the reliability you need?
  • Do you understand UDP amplification and why open UDP services are a DDoS risk?

Chapter 12

Sockets: the API underneath everything

7 min read3 exercises

A socket is the operating system's handle for a network connection, and it's the API every client and server you have ever used is built on, your browser, curl, a database driver, a web framework. Learn the handful of calls and the one gotcha that TCP is a stream of bytes, not messages, and you can build the servers the rest of the web is made of.

The API every program shares

Underneath every HTTP library and web framework is the Berkeley socket API, a small set of system calls, unchanged for decades, that give a program a file-like handle onto a TCP or UDP connection. A server creates a socket, binds it to an address and port, listens, and accepts connections, getting a fresh socket for each one; a client creates a socket and connects to an address; both then send and recv bytes and close when done. That's the whole vocabulary, and this stage's deliverable, an HTTP server on raw sockets, is exactly these calls plus the HTTP parsing of chapter 3. Here is a real, working pair:

It genuinely runs: the server binds to a free port, the client connects (the TCP handshake of chapter 9 happens inside connect), sends a message, and gets it echoed back. Notice the four-tuple printed, (127.0.0.1, 49172) -> (127.0.0.1, 49171), the source and destination addresses and ports that uniquely identify this connection, which is why one listening server can hold thousands of simultaneous connections on a single port: each is a different four-tuple, and each gets its own socket from accept.

The gotcha: it's a stream, not messages

The single most common socket bug follows directly from chapter 9: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries. Your one send of 1000 bytes may arrive as one recv of 1000, or two of 500, or 1000 of one, and two sends may arrive merged into a single recv. The network decides, based on segmentation and timing, not on how you called send. So you cannot assume recv returns a whole message; you must frame the data yourself, and loop until you have all of it. The example does this with a 4-byte length prefix and a recv_exact loop, and HTTP (chapter 3) does it with Content-Length or chunked encoding. Code that does data = conn.recv(4096) and parses data as a complete message works on your laptop and fails in production the first time a message is split across packets, which is a rite of passage every socket programmer goes through once.

Handling many connections

The example serves one connection and exits. A real server must handle many at once, which is where the deliverable's "concurrent connections" requirement bites, and there are three classic approaches:

  • A thread (or process) per connection. Simple to write: accept in a loop, hand each new socket to a worker. It's fine for hundreds of connections but each thread costs memory and the OS struggles past some thousands, the historical C10k problem (ten thousand connections).
  • An event loop (async I/O). One thread watches many sockets at once with select, epoll or kqueue, doing a little work on whichever is ready, never blocking on any one. This is how nginx, Node.js and Python's asyncio handle tens of thousands of connections cheaply, and it's why the networking world went event-driven.
  • A hybrid: a pool of threads, each running an event loop, to use every CPU core, which is what most high-performance servers actually do.

The key realisation is that a networked server spends most of its time waiting, for the next byte, for the client to read, so the scarce resource isn't CPU but the ability to wait on many things at once without a thread tied up per wait. That's the whole motivation for non-blocking I/O.

UDP sockets, and the shape of the two

A UDP socket (chapter 11) uses the same API with a different type (SOCK_DGRAM instead of SOCK_STREAM) and a simpler shape: no listen, no accept, no connection at all, you just sendto an address and recvfrom whoever sends you a datagram. Each recvfrom returns exactly one datagram with its boundary intact, the message-oriented nature from chapter 11, so the stream-framing gotcha doesn't apply, but loss and reordering do. The two socket types are the API's reflection of the two transports: a stream you must frame, or datagrams you must make reliable.

Common traps
  • Treating one recv as one message. Frame your data and loop until you have it all.
  • Forgetting to loop send too (or use sendall): send may write fewer bytes than given.
  • A thread per connection at large scale, hitting the C10k wall instead of using an event loop.
  • Blocking the whole server on one slow client, rather than handling connections concurrently.
  • Leaking sockets by not closing them, running out of file descriptors.
Exercises
Exercise 12.1Find the framing bug

A colleague's server does line = conn.recv(1024).decode() and splits it on newlines to get commands. It works in testing and corrupts commands in production. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?

Show solution

It assumes one recv returns exactly the bytes of one logical chunk, but TCP is a stream: a command may be split across two recv calls (so the first ends mid-command) or several commands may arrive in one recv (and the last may be incomplete). In testing, messages are small and fast, so they usually arrive whole; in production, under real timing and larger payloads, they don't. The fix is to buffer across recv calls and only process complete messages: accumulate incoming bytes, split off whole newline-terminated commands, and keep any trailing partial command in the buffer for the next read. That's the same job as the chapter's length-prefix framing, done with a delimiter instead.

Exercise 12.2Scale the server

A thread-per-connection server handles 500 users fine but falls over at 20,000. What's happening, and what are the options?

Show solution

Each connection has its own OS thread, and 20,000 threads cost gigabytes of stack memory and swamp the scheduler with context switches, the C10k problem. Most of those threads are just waiting on idle sockets, so the memory is pure waste. Options: switch to an event loop (async I/O with epoll/kqueue), where one thread services whichever of the 20,000 sockets has data ready, no thread-per-connection cost; or use a small pool of event-loop threads to use all cores. This is exactly why nginx and Node.js are event-driven, and why Python has asyncio. The deliverable's "concurrent connections" requirement is really an invitation to meet this problem.

Exercise 12.3Trace the calls

List the socket calls, in order, that a browser and a web server make to exchange one request, from the server starting up to the connection closing.

Show solution

Server, at startup: socket() → bind((host, 443)) → listen(), then loops on accept(), which blocks until a client arrives. Browser: socket() → connect((server_ip, 443)), which performs the TCP handshake (chapter 9). Server: accept() returns a new socket for this connection. Then: the browser send()s the HTTP request; the server recv()s it (looping until the full request is read, per framing); the server send()s the response; the browser recv()s it (again looping). Finally: both close() (or keep the socket for the next request, chapter 3's keep-alive). The listening socket stays open for the next client. Every HTTP library you use is doing exactly this underneath.

Checklist
  • Do you know the server calls (socket, bind, listen, accept) and client calls (socket, connect)?
  • Do you frame messages and loop recv, never assuming one read is one message?
  • Do you understand the four-tuple and how one port serves many connections?
  • Do you know when to use threads versus an event loop for concurrency?
  • Could you build the deliverable: an HTTP/1.1 server on raw sockets?
